units.title: Task 1: ModelManager
units.blurb: A mutable struct and its copies, a singleton with side effects, an unclosed FileStream, HttpClient with .Result, Dictionary<object,…>, an empty catch and a God class — everything hiding in a “simple” model manager.

cards.title: Story: renaming into thin air
cards.body:
ModelManager has a button "Add a prefix to every element". RenameAll runs without errors, the compiler is quiet, nothing throws. You open the list and every name is unchanged.

The culprit is one word in a declaration: struct. Let's see why changes "evaporate" with it.

cards.title: A photocopy versus an address
cards.body:
A class is a plate with a house address. Give the plate to a friend and you both walk into the same house: if someone moves the furniture, everyone sees it.

A struct is a sheet of data. Handing it over means making a photocopy. Your friend draws on their copy, and your sheet stays clean.

A copy is made on every assignment, every method argument, every return value and every read from a List.

cards.q: What will this RenameAll do to the _elements list?
options: Nothing: every Rename changes a copy
Rename every element
Throw InvalidOperationException: the collection was modified during enumeration
Fail to compile
cards.explain: The variable e is a copy of the list element. Rename changes the copy, the copy dies at the end of the iteration, and the list is untouched. The compiler does not object: it only forbids assigning to fields of the loop variable, calling methods is allowed.

wrong.1: That is what a class would do: e would be a plate with the address of the same object.
wrong.2: The list does not change at all, so its version has nothing to get out of sync with.
wrong.3: CS1654 is only reported for assigning to a field (e.Name = ...). A method call compiles.

cards.title: The compiler catches half of the cases
cards.body:
A foreach variable is read-only. The compiler rejects e.Name = "X"; with error CS1654. That is good: it tells you straight away that you are writing into a copy.

But it accepts the method call e.Rename("X"). The method changes a field inside, and the compiler does not look at what the method does. The result: the same write into a copy, only without a warning.
cards.deep: By the spec, a foreach iteration variable is a readonly variable. Calling a non-readonly method on a readonly struct variable goes through a hidden defensive copy: not even e itself changes, only a temporary copy of the copy. The same mechanism kicks in for readonly fields and in parameters. Mark the method or the whole struct readonly (C# 7.2/8) and the Name = ... assignment inside the method stops compiling, so the bug surfaces at build time.

cards.q: Which lines will NOT compile if ElementInfo is a struct and _elements is a List<ElementInfo>? Select all.
options: foreach (var e in _elements) e.Name = "X";
foreach (var e in _elements) e.Rename("X");
_elements[0].Name = "X";
_elements[0].Rename("X");
cards.explain: Assigning to a field of a foreach variable is CS1654; assigning to a field of the List indexer result is CS1612 ("not a variable"). Both method calls compile and silently change temporary copies.

cards.task: A piece of ModelManager: the struct, adding elements and bulk renaming. Find the bugs caused by struct copies.

bugs.title: Mutable struct with a mutator method
bugs.why: The struct is copied on every read and every pass, and Rename changes only the copy it was called on. Changes get lost silently.

bugs.title: ChildIds: null by default and shared by all copies
bugs.why: For default(ElementInfo) and for an element whose JSON lacks the field, the list is null, and the first access throws NullReferenceException. And all copies share one list: each copy has its own name but the same children.

bugs.title: Two independent copies in two collections
bugs.why: The list and the dictionary get different photocopies. Change an element in one collection and the other keeps returning stale data.

bugs.title: foreach changes a copy
bugs.why: Rename runs on a copy of the element, and the list does not change. RenameAll silently does nothing.

cards.q: The author "fixes" RenameAll with an index loop. What now?
cards.code:
for (int i = 0; i < _elements.Count; i++)
    _elements[i].Rename(prefix + _elements[i].Name);
options: It compiles and still changes nothing
It works: the indexer gives access to the element itself
Compile error CS1612
cards.explain: The List<T> indexer is a get method, and it returns a copy. Rename changes that temporary copy. CS1612 would only appear for a direct field assignment: _elements[i].Name = ...

wrong.1: That is how an array behaves: arr[i] is the slot itself. A List returns a value through get.
wrong.2: CS1612 is about assigning to a field. Calling a method on a temporary value is allowed.

cards.title: An array hands you the slot, a list hands you a copy
cards.body:
For an array, arr[i] is the memory slot itself, so arr[i].Rename("X") really changes the element. For List<T>, the indexer is an ordinary method that returns a value, that is, a copy.

The reliable recipe for a list of structs: read, modify, write back.
cards.deep: Modern .NET has CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list) (.NET 5+): it gives a Span<T> over the internal array, and span[i] is a reference to the element. That is an optimization for hot paths, not a way to write business logic, and Unity (the .NET Standard 2.1 profile) does not have it. Reading _elements[i].Name also formally copies the whole struct; the JIT often removes that, but it does not have to.

cards.q: Fix the renaming: change the copy and write it back into BOTH collections.
cards.explain: As long as ElementInfo is a struct, each collection holds its own copy, and both must be updated. The dictionary key is the element Id, not the list index. This is clumsy and easy to forget, so the better fix is to change the type itself (next cards).

cards.q: What will the list see after this code?
options: The old name, but 42 appears in ChildIds
Name "X" and 42 in ChildIds
Nothing changes
Name "X", and ChildIds unchanged
cards.explain: Copying a struct copies the reference to the list, not the list itself. The copy has its own Name, but ChildIds points to the same object. Half value, half reference: confusion guaranteed.

wrong.1: Name was copied by value, so the change stayed in a.
wrong.2: ChildIds is shared by the copy and the original, so Add is visible.
wrong.3: It is the other way round: Name belongs to the copy, the list is shared.

cards.title: How to fix it: a class or an immutable struct
cards.body:
There are two honest options.

1. A class. ElementInfo is an entity with an identity (Id) that gets modified and passed between parts of the system. That is reference-type behavior: one plate, one house.

2. A readonly struct. If you need a struct, make it immutable: to change it, create a new one and put it in place of the old one.
cards.deep: The .NET Framework Design Guidelines say a struct should logically represent a single value, be small (the rule of thumb is under 16 bytes), be immutable and rarely get boxed. Here, on a 64-bit platform, it is about 48 bytes (an int, two references and a Bounds made of two Vector3s), so every copy moves three quarters of a 64-byte cache line. The with expression for ordinary structs arrived in C# 10; Unity (C# 9) does not have it, so you write a WithName method by hand. A mutable List<int> inside a readonly struct is still mutable: readonly protects the reference field, not the list contents (prefer IReadOnlyList<int>).

cards.q: Match an operation on the ElementInfo struct with what really happens.
pairs: A temporary copy changes, the list does not
The subscriber gets its own copy

cards.q: Which fix for ElementInfo suits this code best?
options: Make ElementInfo a class (or a readonly struct replaced as a whole)
Keep the mutable struct and pass it by ref everywhere
Add this = new ElementInfo() to Rename
cards.explain: A model element has an identity and changes over time, so a class is the natural choice. If compactness matters, use an immutable struct: then changing it "by mistake in a copy" is simply impossible.

wrong.1: ref does not work with foreach, the List indexer or events, which is exactly where the bugs are. One forgotten spot and the copy is back.
wrong.2: Assigning this inside a struct method changes the very copy the method was called on. The problem stays.

lessons.title: Singleton, constructor and handles
lessons.sub: One static line that kills the whole type

cards.title: Story: a type that died for good
cards.body:
Everything worked in the editor. In the build, the console shows TypeInitializationException at startup, and from then on every access to ModelManager fails with the same exception. Reloading the scene does not help, only restarting the app does.

It all comes down to one line: public static ModelManager Instance = new ModelManager();

cards.title: The static initializer gets one attempt
cards.body:
A static field initializer runs inside the type initializer (the static constructor). The CLR runs it once, when the type is first used.

If it throws, the CLR wraps the exception in TypeInitializationException and remembers the failure. There is no second attempt: the type is "poisoned" for the rest of the process lifetime (in Unity, until the domain reloads).

And this constructor does a lot of risky things: it opens a file and subscribes to SelectionService.Current. If Current does not exist yet, you get a NullReferenceException right inside the type initializer.
cards.deep: The real cause sits in InnerException; the top-level message only says "The type initializer for 'ModelManager' threw an exception". If the class has no explicit static constructor, the type is marked beforefieldinit, and the CLR may run the initialization at any moment before the first static field access, so its order relative to SelectionService is not guaranteed at all. In Unity with domain reload disabled (Enter Play Mode Options), statics survive exiting Play Mode: both a healthy and a "poisoned" type stay until scripts recompile.

cards.q: Put in order how one static line turns into a TypeInitializationException.
items: Code accesses ModelManager.Instance for the first time
The CLR runs the ModelManager type initializer
new ModelManager() is called
SelectionService.Current is still null, so NullReferenceException
The CLR wraps it in TypeInitializationException and remembers the failure
cards.explain: The type initializer runs once. Its exception becomes "permanent": every later access to the type throws the same TypeInitializationException.

cards.q: The first access to ModelManager.Instance failed. What happens on a second access a minute later, when SelectionService.Current already exists?
options: TypeInitializationException again
Initialization runs again and succeeds
Instance returns null without an exception
cards.explain: The CLR does not retry a type initializer. The failure is remembered, and the type stays unusable for the rest of the process (domain) lifetime. That is why side effects in static initialization are so dangerous.

wrong.1: There is no retry: a static constructor runs at most once, even if it fails.
wrong.2: It never gets to the field: accessing any static member of the type throws.

cards.task: The start of ModelManager: the singleton, the constructor and log writing. Find the lifecycle and resource bugs.

bugs.title: Owns a FileStream but is not IDisposable
bugs.why: The class holds a file handle and has no way to close it: there is no Dispose, so nobody outside can release the resource.

bugs.title: Singleton: a public mutable field and risky static initialization
bugs.why: Any code can overwrite Instance. An exception in the constructor becomes a TypeInitializationException and poisons the type for good.

bugs.title: A public constructor on a singleton
bugs.why: Anyone can create a second instance: it opens log.txt again (IOException) and subscribes to the event twice.

bugs.title: The FileStream is never closed
bugs.why: The handle stays taken until the process ends, with FileShare.Read by default: a second instance or another process cannot open the file for writing. The relative path depends on the current directory.

bugs.title: A subscription in the constructor that nobody removes
bugs.why: If Current is still null, you get an NRE during type initialization. The subscription is never removed: SelectionService keeps the object alive, and this escapes from a half-built constructor.

bugs.title: Writes without Flush on the main thread
bugs.why: FileStream buffers data (4 KB by default): if the process crashes, the last log lines are lost. The synchronous write blocks whichever thread raised the event.

cards.title: A file handle is a room key
cards.body:
Opening a file means getting a room key from the OS. While you hold the key, the OS knows the room is taken and decides who else may come in. Here the key is taken in the constructor and never given back.

new FileStream(path, FileMode.Append) opens the file write-only with FileShare.Read: others may read, but not write. A second new ModelManager() or a second running process gets an IOException: "the file is being used by another process".
cards.deep: The FileStream(string, FileMode) constructor uses FileAccess.Write for Append (ReadWrite for the other modes) and FileShare.Read, with a 4096-byte buffer. Sharing modes are strictly enforced on Windows; on Unix, .NET emulates them with advisory locks, so behavior there can differ. SafeFileHandle has a finalizer, so the GC will eventually close a "forgotten" stream, but not here: the object lives in a static field forever. A relative "log.txt" in Unity goes to the process current directory (the project folder in the editor, anyone's guess in a build, and on mobile you often cannot write there at all); the right place is Application.persistentDataPath.

cards.q: A test writes var m = new ModelManager(); while Instance already exists. What most likely happens on Windows?
options: IOException: log.txt is already open for writing by the first instance
The second instance silently replaces Instance
Both instances write to the same log without problems
cards.explain: The first instance holds the file with FileShare.Read, so others may only read. A second FileStream opened for writing hits a sharing violation. Instance does not change: this is just one more object.

wrong.1: The constructor never writes to Instance. You get a second object next to it, not a replacement.
wrong.2: Shared writing is forbidden by FileShare.Read, which is the default.

cards.title: A subscription is a leash
cards.body:
Current.SelectionChanged += OnSelectionChanged puts a delegate into the event, and the delegate holds a reference to this. That is a leash from SelectionService to ModelManager: as long as the event source lives, so does the subscriber, even if nobody needs it anymore.

Subscribing in the constructor also lets this escape before the object is fully built: an event can arrive while fields are not yet initialized.
cards.deep: For a static singleton the leak is less visible (it lives forever anyway), but it shows up as soon as a second instance, tests or a scene reload appear: old objects keep receiving events, and the handler runs twice. The rule: whoever subscribes also unsubscribes, symmetrically (Init/Dispose, in Unity OnEnable/OnDisable). Weak events (the weak event pattern) are a crutch for cases where you cannot control the subscriber lifetime.

cards.q: What is wrong with subscribing SelectionService.Current.SelectionChanged += OnSelectionChanged right in the constructor? Select all.
options: If Current is still null, the constructor throws NullReferenceException
There is no unsubscribe, so SelectionService keeps ModelManager alive
this becomes visible outside before the constructor finishes
The compiler forbids subscribing to events in a constructor
cards.explain: Subscribing in a constructor is syntactically fine, but it is a hidden dependency on global state, a leak without unsubscribing, and an "escaping this". Move the subscription to an explicit Init and unsubscribe in Dispose.

cards.q: Rewrite the singleton safely: the field cannot be overwritten, the constructor cannot be called from outside, the subscription can be removed.
cards.explain: readonly prevents overwriting the field, a private constructor prevents a second instance, and -= removes the leash. Everything risky moved into an explicit Init: if it fails, the type is not poisoned and the call can be retried.

cards.title: For seniors: Lazy remembers errors too
cards.body:
Lazy<T> gives you laziness and thread safety, but in the default mode (ExecutionAndPublication) it caches the factory exception: if the constructor failed, every later .Value throws the same exception. The poisoning did not go away, it just moved from the type into the field.

So the main cure is not "Lazy instead of new" but a constructor without side effects plus explicit initialization.
cards.deep: LazyThreadSafetyMode.PublicationOnly does not cache exceptions, but it allows several threads to run the factory in parallel. Even better is to drop the global singleton altogether: inject ModelManager through constructors (a DI container such as VContainer or Zenject in Unity) or from a scene composition root. Then the dependency on SelectionService is visible in the signature, it can be replaced in a test, and you control the creation order, not the CLR.

cards.q: Match the problem with the fix.
pairs: Side effects in the type initializer

lessons.title: Loading: HttpClient, .Result and atomicity
lessons.sub: The game freezes, sockets run out, data drifts apart

cards.title: Story: three complaints about one button
cards.body:
The "Load model" button calls Load(url). QA files three tickets:

1. While the model loads, the game freezes.
2. After frequent reloads, connection errors pour in.
3. Loading the same model again throws ArgumentException, and search finds elements that are missing from the dictionary.

All three live in nine lines of one method.

cards.title: HttpClient is a phone exchange, not a call
cards.body:
HttpClient is meant to be an exchange you set up once and call through many times: inside it has a connection pool and reuses sockets that are already open.

A new HttpClient per call is a new exchange with its own pool. Old connections are not reused, and closed ones linger for minutes in TIME_WAIT. With frequent calls you run out of local ports: SocketException, even though the network is fine.
cards.deep: Here the old client is not even disposed: its connections close only when its finalizer runs, whenever the GC gets to it. But using (var c = new HttpClient()) per request is no cure either: the sockets still go to TIME_WAIT. The right way is one long-lived instance (static) or IHttpClientFactory. In modern .NET a long-lived client has its own trap: it does not notice DNS changes; SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime fixes that. In Unity, networking is often written with UnityWebRequest; on WebGL HttpClient does not work at all (no sockets).

cards.q: Load is called every couple of seconds. What will the line _http = new HttpClient() eventually cause?
options: Sockets pile up, and new connections start failing with SocketException
Nothing: HttpClient is a lightweight object with no resources
A compiler warning that stops the build
cards.explain: Each client opens its own connections and does not share them. Closed connections keep the port in TIME_WAIT for a while. Under load this is port exhaustion, a classic .NET mistake.

wrong.1: Inside HttpClient there is a handler with a connection pool and OS sockets. It is a heavy object.
wrong.2: The compiler notices nothing here. The failure only shows up at runtime, under load.

cards.title: .Result: standing at the door until the parcel arrives
cards.body:
GetStringAsync is a delivery order: it immediately returns a "receipt" (a Task). .Result means "I will stand at the door doing nothing until it arrives". If the one standing is Unity's main thread, the whole game freezes: no frames, no input.

The second problem: the error does not arrive as is but wrapped in AggregateException, and catch (HttpRequestException) will not catch it.
cards.deep: HttpClient itself uses ConfigureAwait(false) internally, so this exact line usually "only" freezes the thread for the duration of the request. But wrap the call in your own async method without ConfigureAwait(false), call .Result on it from the main thread, and you get the classic deadlock: the continuation waits for the main thread through Unity's SynchronizationContext, and the main thread waits for the continuation. .GetAwaiter().GetResult() does not wrap the exception in AggregateException, but it blocks just the same, so it is not a fix.

cards.q: The server returned 404. Which exception reaches the caller of Load?
cards.code: var json = _http.GetStringAsync(url).Result;
options: AggregateException with an HttpRequestException inside
HttpRequestException as is
None: Result returns an empty string
cards.explain: Task.Result wraps the task error in AggregateException. The real cause is in InnerException. With await you would get the original HttpRequestException.

wrong.1: That is what await would give you. The blocking .Result wraps the exception.
wrong.2: GetStringAsync checks the status code and fails the task for 404.

cards.task: The fields and the load method of ModelManager. Find the bugs: network, blocking, JSON data, atomicity and the key type.

bugs.title: A dictionary keyed by object
bugs.why: Every int Id is boxed on insert and on every lookup: extra allocations. Type safety is gone too: store a long and you will not find it by int.

bugs.title: A new HttpClient on every call
bugs.why: Each client starts its own connection pool, and the old one is never released. With frequent loads, sockets pile up and ports run out.

bugs.title: Synchronous loading through .Result
bugs.why: The thread stands still during the request: on Unity's main thread the game freezes. Errors arrive in AggregateException, and there is no cancellation or timeout.

bugs.title: DeserializeObject can return null
bugs.why: For the JSON "null" or an empty response the result is null, and foreach throws NullReferenceException.

bugs.title: A repeated Load duplicates elements
bugs.why: The method clears nothing: a second call appends the same elements to _elements again.

bugs.title: Add throws in the middle of the loop
bugs.why: On a duplicate Id, Dictionary.Add throws ArgumentException. Some elements are already in _elements but not in _byId: the collections are out of sync.

cards.q: The model is already loaded. Load is called a second time with the same JSON. What happens? Select all.
options: _elements grows by one element
_byId stays the same
The caller gets an ArgumentException
_elements doubles
cards.explain: The first element makes it into _elements, then _byId.Add on an existing Id throws ArgumentException and the loop stops. The list has N+1 elements, the dictionary has N. A "half-done" operation is exactly what a lack of atomicity looks like.

cards.title: Atomicity: pack a new box next to the old one
cards.body:
Do not move items one by one into a box people are already taking things from. Pack a new box next to it, check it, and only then swap it in for the old one in a single move.

Then any error (network, bad JSON, a duplicate Id) leaves the old data intact, and a repeated call creates no duplicates.
cards.deep: Swapping two fields (_elements = list; _byId = byId;) is atomic for a single thread. If readers live on other threads, they might see the new list with the old dictionary; then keep both in one immutable snapshot object and swap a single reference (Volatile.Write/Interlocked.Exchange). In Unity, the continuation after await returns to the main thread by default, so the swap happens where the data is read, and there is no race.

cards.q: Build a correct load: one client for the whole app and a dictionary without boxing.
cards.explain: One static readonly client reuses connections. Dictionary<int, ...> does not box keys. The new collections are built separately and swapped in only after every check, so an error never leaves the data "half loaded".

cards.title: object as a key: every number in its own box
cards.body:
To put an int where an object is expected, the runtime boxes the number into a box on the heap. Dictionary<object, ...> does this on every Add and every _byId[id]: garbage for the GC on every lookup.

It works: a boxed int is compared by value. But the compiler no longer checks the key type.
cards.code:
_byId.Add(5, e);           // the key is a boxed int
_byId.ContainsKey(5L);     // false: long 5 is not int 5
cards.deep: Int32.Equals(object) returns true only if the argument is also a boxed int; a boxed long or short with the same number is not equal. Dictionary<int, T> uses EqualityComparer<int>.Default, which works with int directly, without boxing. In Unity this shows up in the Profiler as GC Alloc in hot spots like the selection handler.

cards.q: What does the last line return?
options: false
true
It throws InvalidCastException
cards.explain: The key is a boxed int 7, and the lookup uses a boxed short 7. These are different types, and Int32.Equals(object) returns false. With Dictionary<int, string>, the short would widen to int implicitly, and the lookup would succeed.

wrong.1: The numbers are equal, but they are boxed as different types. For an object key, those are different keys.
wrong.2: There is no cast here: the dictionary just compares objects with Equals.

cards.q: Put the steps of a reliable model reload in order.
items: Download the JSON asynchronously with the shared HttpClient (with a cancellation token)
Deserialize and replace null with an empty list
Build a new dictionary, checking for duplicate Ids
Swap _elements and _byId at once
Notify subscribers that the model has been updated
cards.explain: Everything that can fail happens before the swap. Subscribers are called last, once the data is consistent.

cards.q: Match the line of Load with its problem.
pairs: Boxing an int on every lookup

lessons.title: Search, events and an empty catch
lessons.sub: Selection "just doesn't work", and the log is empty

cards.title: Story: silence instead of an error
cards.body:
The user clicks a pipe in the scene. The properties panel does not update. The selection log is empty, the console has not a single error. Five clicks, ten: silence.

There are errors, and more than one. A single line eats them all: catch (Exception) { }.

cards.title: An empty catch is a garbage chute for errors
cards.body:
catch (Exception) { } catches everything and drops it down the chute without looking. An unknown id, no subscribers, a locked log file, an error in someone else's handler: to the user it all looks the same, "it doesn't work". To the developer it also looks the same: not a single log line.

The rule: catch only the exceptions you expect and know how to handle, and let the rest fly on, or at least reach the log.

cards.q: Which problems does this empty catch silently hide? Select all.
options: KeyNotFoundException for an unknown id
NullReferenceException when nobody subscribed to ElementSelected
IOException while writing the log
A compile error in the handler
cards.explain: Anything thrown at runtime inside the try vanishes without a trace. Compile errors never make it to runtime, so catch has nothing to do with them.

cards.task: Name search and the selection handler from ModelManager. Find the bugs: strings, the dictionary, the event, the log and error handling.

bugs.title: ToLower in a loop: allocations, culture, null
bugs.why: Every iteration creates two new strings, and name.ToLower() is recomputed each time. ToLower depends on the culture (the Turkish I), and Name == null throws NullReferenceException.

bugs.title: Dictionary indexer with an unknown id
bugs.why: _byId[id] throws KeyNotFoundException if the element is missing (a click on another model's object, a selection before loading). Use TryGetValue.

bugs.title: Raising the event without a null check
bugs.why: With no subscribers the event field is null, and the call throws NullReferenceException. A subscriber exception also aborts the method, so the log line is never written.

bugs.title: Logging: DateTime.Now, concatenation, no Flush
bugs.why: Local time jumps with time zone and daylight saving changes, and the date format depends on the culture. Strings and a byte array are allocated on every click, and an unflushed buffer is lost on a crash.

bugs.title: An empty catch (Exception)
bugs.why: It swallows every error above without a trace: selection "just doesn't work", and the cause is nowhere in the log or the console.

cards.title: ToLower: expensive and country-dependent
cards.body:
name.ToLower() inside the loop makes a new string on every iteration, even though name never changes. _elements[i].Name.ToLower() is one more string per element. With 100,000 elements that is 200,000 garbage strings per search.

Worse, ToLower() uses the current culture. In the Turkish culture the capital I becomes a dotless "ı", so searching for "id" will not find "ID".
cards.code:
// no allocations and no culture dependency
n.IndexOf(name, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) >= 0
cards.deep: The string.Contains(string, StringComparison) overload exists in .NET Core 2.1+ and .NET Standard 2.1 (Unity 2021.2+); IndexOf(..., StringComparison) works everywhere, including old Mono. OrdinalIgnoreCase compares character codes with simple case folding, which is exactly what identifiers and element names need. For natural-language search (diacritics and the like) use CompareInfo.IndexOf with the right culture. If searches are frequent, build an index (a dictionary by normalized name or a prefix tree) instead of a linear scan.

cards.q: The current culture is tr-TR. An element is called "ID-42". What does FindByName("id") return?
cards.code: if (_elements[i].Name.ToLower().Contains(name.ToLower()))
options: An empty list: "ID-42".ToLower() gives "ıd-42"
A list with this element
It throws CultureNotFoundException
cards.explain: In the Turkish alphabet I and i have different partners: the capital I becomes a lowercase dotless ı. So "ıd-42" does not contain "id". This is the famous "Turkish I problem", a reason to always pass StringComparison explicitly.

wrong.1: It would be found with OrdinalIgnoreCase or the invariant culture, but not with ToLower() under tr-TR.
wrong.2: The tr-TR culture exists, so nothing is thrown: you just get the "wrong" result.

cards.q: Fix FindByName: no extra strings, no culture, no crash on null.
cards.explain: The null check protects against elements without a name. OrdinalIgnoreCase creates no new strings and does not depend on the culture. Ordinal would be case-sensitive, and CurrentCulture would bring back the Turkish problem.

cards.title: CountClashes: every pair twice
cards.body: The double loop runs over every i and every j. The pair "pipe 1, beam 2" is checked as (1, 2) and again as (2, 1). The i != j condition only removes comparing an element with itself. The result is exactly twice the truth, and so is the work.
cards.deep: Even with j = i + 1 the algorithm is O(n²): for 50,000 elements that is about 1.25 billion checks. Real clash detection first prunes pairs in a broad phase (a uniform grid, a BVH or octree, or sweep-and-prune along one axis), and only then tests the candidates. A detail for a hot loop: _elements[i].Box through the List indexer copies the whole 48-byte struct for one field, and Bounds.Intersects takes Bounds by value, which is another copy.

cards.q: Which line makes CountClashes count every pair twice?
cards.explain: The inner loop starts at 0, so every pair shows up in both orders. Start at j = i + 1 and the i != j check is no longer needed, while each pair is counted once.

cards.q: Three boxes, all three overlapping each other. What does the original CountClashes return?
cards.explain: There are three real pairs: (0,1), (0,2), (1,2). A loop over every j, skipping only self-comparison, counts each twice: 3 x 2 = 6. Nine would require dropping the i != j check as well.

wrong.1: Three is the correct answer for j = i + 1. The original code counts each pair in both orders.
wrong.2: 9 = 3 x 3 would include comparing each box with itself, but i != j filters that out.

cards.title: An event with no subscribers is null
cards.body:
An event field nobody subscribed to is null. Calling ElementSelected(e) then throws NullReferenceException. The short form ElementSelected?.Invoke(e) calls subscribers only if there are any.

The second trap: if the first subscriber throws, the remaining subscribers are not called, and the code after the call (the log write) does not run.
cards.deep: ?.Invoke reads the field once, so it also closes the race "checked for null, but the last subscriber unsubscribed on another thread before the call". A multicast delegate calls subscribers one by one and stops at the first exception. If the handlers are foreign and unreliable, iterate GetInvocationList() and wrap each one in a try/catch with logging. As for the log: write the time as DateTime.UtcNow.ToString("o") (ISO 8601, independent of time zone and culture), and write through a StreamWriter with WriteLine instead of a manual Encoding.GetBytes per line.

cards.q: Which version of the handler is better?
options: TryGetValue, then ElementSelected?.Invoke(e), then the log write, with a catch only for IOException that calls Debug.LogException
Keep catch (Exception) { }, but add a retry
catch (Exception ex) { throw ex; }
cards.explain: Expected situations (no such id, no subscribers) are checked up front, without exceptions. Only what can really happen to the file is caught, and it gets logged. Everything else is an honest error that people will see.

wrong.1: Retrying a swallowed error is the same silence, only twice.
wrong.2: throw ex; also resets the stack trace. If you must rethrow, use throw; but here there is no reason to catch and rethrow at all.

cards.q: Match the symptom with the cause.
pairs: Selection does nothing, the log is empty
Clicking a foreign object gives KeyNotFoundException
NRE when the properties panel is closed
Twice as many clashes as there are
The inner loop starts at j = 0
Log timestamps jump by an hour

lessons.title: Final: ModelManager
lessons.sub: Find the bugs in the full listing

cards.task: This is the whole ModelManager sent for review. Flag as many bugs as you can: the mutable struct, the singleton, resources, loading, search, events and error handling. You need at least 16.

bugs.title: Mutable struct with a mutator method
bugs.why: ElementInfo is copied on every List read, every pass and every assignment, and Rename changes only its own copy. Changes get lost silently, and copies in different places drift apart.

bugs.title: ChildIds: null by default and shared by copies
bugs.why: For default(ElementInfo) and when the JSON lacks the field, the list is null, so access throws NullReferenceException. All copies of the struct share the same list: half value, half reference.

bugs.title: Singleton: a public non-readonly field and risky static initialization
bugs.why: Anyone can overwrite Instance. An exception in the constructor becomes a TypeInitializationException, and the type stays poisoned for the rest of the process lifetime.

bugs.title: Shared collections without synchronization
bugs.why: If Load runs in the background while a selection arrives on the main thread, the List and the Dictionary are read during a write: a race, garbage or exceptions.

bugs.title: A dictionary keyed by object
bugs.why: Every int Id is boxed on insert and on every lookup, so every click allocates. The key type is not checked: long 5 will not find int 5.

bugs.title: A new HttpClient on every Load
bugs.why: Each client keeps its own connection pool, and the old one is neither released nor reused. With frequent loads, sockets pile up and ports run out.

bugs.title: A public constructor on a singleton
bugs.why: A second instance can be created: it opens log.txt again (IOException because of FileShare.Read) and subscribes to selection once more.

bugs.title: The FileStream is never closed
bugs.why: There is no IDisposable, and the handle stays taken until the process ends. The relative path depends on the current directory, and an unflushed buffer is lost on a crash.

bugs.title: A subscription in the constructor with no unsubscribe
bugs.why: If SelectionService.Current is still null, you get an NRE inside type initialization. Nobody removes the subscription: the source keeps the object alive, and this escapes from a half-built constructor.

bugs.title: Synchronous loading through .Result
bugs.why: The thread waits for the network: on Unity's main thread the game freezes. Errors arrive in AggregateException, there is no cancellation or timeout, and combined with your own async code a deadlock is possible.

bugs.title: DeserializeObject can return null
bugs.why: For the JSON "null" or an empty response, elements is null, and foreach throws NullReferenceException.

bugs.title: Load clears nothing
bugs.why: A repeated call appends the elements to _elements again: duplicates in search and in clash counting.

bugs.title: Dictionary.Add throws mid-loop
bugs.why: A duplicate Id throws ArgumentException. Some elements are already in the list but not in the dictionary: the collections are out of sync, and the operation is not atomic.

bugs.title: RenameAll changes copies
bugs.why: The foreach variable is a copy of the struct, Rename changes it, and the list stays the same. The method silently does nothing.

bugs.title: ToLower in a loop
bugs.why: Two new strings per element, and name.ToLower() is recomputed every time. It depends on the culture (the Turkish I) and throws NullReferenceException on an element without a name.

bugs.title: Every pair is counted twice
bugs.why: The inner loop starts at j = 0 and checks both (i, j) and (j, i): the result is twice the truth. Use j = i + 1, and a spatial index for large models.

bugs.title: Indexer with an unknown id
bugs.why: _byId[id] throws KeyNotFoundException if there is no such element. Use TryGetValue.

bugs.title: The event is raised without a null check
bugs.why: With no subscribers, ElementSelected is null, so NullReferenceException. A subscriber exception aborts the method, and the log is not written.

bugs.title: Logging: DateTime.Now, concatenation, a synchronous write
bugs.why: Local time and its format depend on the time zone and culture, and every click allocates strings and an array. The write is synchronous, with no Flush and no lock.

bugs.title: An empty catch (Exception)
bugs.why: It swallows every error above without a trace: selection "just doesn't work", and the log and console are empty.

cards.q: Which bugs in the listing throw no exceptions at all and simply give a wrong result? Select all.
options: RenameAll changes copies of the struct
CountClashes counts every pair twice
The object key in the dictionary boxes an int
A repeated Load with the same data
cards.explain: RenameAll silently does nothing, CountClashes silently doubles the answer, boxing silently creates garbage. A repeated Load is the loud one: Dictionary.Add throws ArgumentException on the very first duplicate.

cards.q: On which line is the NullReferenceException thrown that becomes a TypeInitializationException if SelectionService does not exist yet?
cards.explain: Accessing Current.SelectionChanged while Current == null throws an NRE. Since the constructor is called from a static field initializer, the CLR wraps it in TypeInitializationException, and the type becomes unusable for the rest of the process lifetime.

cards.q: Which of these does NOT save Load from socket exhaustion?
options: using (var c = new HttpClient()) per request
One static readonly HttpClient for the whole app
IHttpClientFactory, which reuses handlers
cards.explain: Dispose closes the connections, but closed sockets still linger in TIME_WAIT for a while, and clients do not share a connection pool. Reusing one client or a handler factory is the right way.

wrong.1: This is the recommended option: connections get reused. In modern .NET, add PooledConnectionLifetime so DNS changes are noticed.
wrong.2: The factory keeps and reuses handlers with their pools; that is what it was built for.

cards.q: Two one-line fixes: make the element a reference type and raise the event safely.
cards.explain: With a class, foreach, the List indexer and the event all pass a reference to the same object, and RenameAll starts working. The ?. operator raises the event only if there are subscribers and reads the field once.

cards.q: Put the lifecycle of the fixed ModelManager in order.
items: Create the object: a constructor without side effects
Init: open the log and subscribe to SelectionService
await LoadAsync: download, validate and swap the collections at once
Work: search, selection, clash counting
Dispose: unsubscribe from the event and close the log
cards.explain: Everything that can fail or holds resources moved out of the constructor into explicit steps. Every "take" (subscription, file) has a matching "give back" in Dispose.

cards.q: Match the bug with the fix.
Why is this listing a good interview task, even though it compiles without a single error?
options: Most of its bugs show up at runtime: struct copies, resources, networking, swallowed errors
The C# compiler will find these mistakes during the build anyway
These are only style issues, they do not affect behavior
cards.explain: The compiler only catches a direct assignment to a field of a copy (CS1654, CS1612). Everything else (silent copies, leaked handles and sockets, blocking, races and an empty catch) is visible only to someone who understands how the code behaves at runtime.

wrong.1: Calling a mutating method on a copy, .Result, an empty catch and new HttpClient are not errors to the compiler.
wrong.2: Quite the opposite: nearly every item changes behavior, from a no-op RenameAll to a frozen game.

units.title: Task 2: ClashService
units.blurb: A closure in a loop, async void, dictionary keys, collections, recursion, exceptions and Unity’s “fake null” — a dozen bugs in one clash-detection service.

lessons.title: Loop closures and async void
lessons.sub: Why the service found zero clashes

cards.title: Story: zero clashes
cards.body:
A building model has hundreds of pipes and beams that cross each other. ClashService starts 8 tasks, and each one checks its own "bucket" of elements. The run finishes without errors and reports: no clashes. But there are clashes.

This is the sneakiest kind of bug: nothing crashed, the answer looks fine, it is just wrong. Let's see where it comes from.

cards.title: A lambda holds the box, not the value
cards.body:
A lambda does not copy a variable. It remembers the box the variable lives in. In a for loop there is one box i for all iterations. The task from Task.Run peeks into the box only when the thread pool gets to it, and by then the eight-iteration loop has usually finished. The box holds 8.

In foreach every iteration gets a fresh box (since C# 5), so that trap does not exist there.
cards.deep: The compiler hoists the captured variable into a hidden closure class (a display class). With for, the variable is declared before the loop body, so there is one instance. With foreach (since C# 5) and with variables declared inside the body, a new instance is created per iteration. The behavior is non-deterministic: a task that managed to start before the next i++ sees a smaller number. That is why the bug "floats" between runs.

cards.q: What will ProcessChunk most often receive in the chunk parameter?
cards.code:
for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++)
    tasks.Add(Task.Run(() => ProcessChunk(elements, i)));
options: 8 for every task
0, 1, 2, ... 7 in order
Each gets its own number, but in random order
cards.explain: By the time the tasks start, the loop has usually finished, and the shared variable is 8. The filter e.Id % 8 == 8 is never true, so no pairs are found at all.

wrong.1: That would happen if every lambda saw its own value. But there is one box for all.
wrong.2: Random order would need copies. Here the variable is shared, so almost every task sees the final value.

cards.task: Here is the launch and the processing of one bucket. Find the bugs: they are about closures, async, lazy enumeration and shared state.

bugs.title: async void
bugs.why: The caller cannot wait for completion or catch the exception. If ProcessChunk throws, Completed never fires, and the error goes to the SynchronizationContext: in Unity it is just a line in the console, in .NET without a context the process crashes.

bugs.title: Closure over the loop variable i
bugs.why: Tasks see the shared i, usually already 8. The chunk filter selects nothing, and the service silently finds zero clashes.

bugs.title: Id % 8 buckets split the pairs
bugs.why: Elements from different buckets are never compared with each other, so some clashes can never be found. For negative Ids the remainder is negative too.

bugs.title: Lazy sequence enumerated many times
bugs.why: mine is a Where recipe, not a list. The inner loop re-runs the filter for every outer element: n² predicate calls, and if the source is lazy too, repeated computation.

bugs.title: Race on List.Add
bugs.why: List<T> is not thread-safe. Eight threads corrupt its internal array at the same time: items get lost, exceptions happen.

bugs.title: Non-atomic counter
bugs.why: The ++ operation is read, add, write. Threads overwrite each other's values, so the count ends up too low. Also, the name _processed promises one thing but counts another.

cards.q: Fix the closure: every task needs its own copy of the number.
cards.explain: The copy is declared inside the loop body, so each iteration gets a new box. The lambda must use the copy, not i.

cards.title: async void: a call with no callback number
cards.body:
async Task returns a "receipt": you can wait for completion and learn how it ended. async void gives no receipt. The caller cannot await, and a failure has nobody to catch it.

There is one legitimate use: event handlers (in Unity that includes message methods like async void Start()). Everything else should be async Task.
cards.deep: An exception from async void has no Task to live in, so it is rethrown through the SynchronizationContext captured when the method started. In Unity that is UnitySynchronizationContext: the exception runs in its queue on the main thread, Unity logs it to the console, and the game keeps going as if nothing happened. Without a context (a console app, a pool thread) it is thrown on the thread pool as unhandled, and the .NET process terminates. Either way, the code after the failed await never runs: Completed never fires, and whoever waits for it waits forever. Also, a test or the caller cannot await such a method.

cards.q: What changes for the caller once RunAsync becomes async Task?
options: It can await and catch exceptions with try/catch
The method gets faster
The method starts running on the main thread
cards.explain: A Task gives the caller a point to wait on and a channel for errors. Speed and thread are not affected.

wrong.1: Speed is the same. Only what you get back changes.
wrong.2: The executing thread is decided by await and the synchronization context, not by the return type.

cards.title: Lazy filters and a shared list
cards.body:
Where does not filter, it writes down a recipe. Every foreach over it cooks the dish again. Nest one foreach in another and the recipe runs once per outer element.

The second lesson from the kitchen: eight cooks must not write into one notebook at the same time. Either queue up for the notebook (lock), or give each cook their own notebook and glue them together later.
cards.code:
var all = elements.ToList();            // once
var mine = all.Where(...).ToList();     // a ready list
var local = new List<Clash>();          // one per task

cards.q: Which operations are unsafe when several threads run them on shared fields? Pick all that apply.
options: _clashes.Add(clash)
_processed++
var n = 5;  (a local variable)
Interlocked.Increment(ref _processed)
cards.explain: Add and ++ read and write shared state in several steps. A local variable belongs to its own thread, and Interlocked is atomic.

cards.q: Put the steps of a reliable RunAsync in order.
items: Turn elements into a list once (ToList)
In the loop, make a local copy of the bucket number
Start 8 tasks, each with its own local list
Wait for all of them with await Task.WhenAll
Merge the local lists into _clashes
cards.explain: First pin down the data and the numbers, then work in parallel with no shared writes, and only after waiting for everyone collect the result on one thread.

cards.q: Match each bug with its fix.
pairs: A local copy inside the body
Lazy Where in a double loop

cards.title: For seniors: what else is wrong with the split
cards.body: Even after the fixes, the algorithm has a hole. Since pairs are compared only inside a bucket, elements from different buckets never meet. It is better to split the outer loop between tasks (who gets which a) and let the inner loop run over all b. Even better, avoid n² entirely: build a spatial index (a grid, a BVH) and test only neighbors.
cards.deep: Note that splitting by Id % 8 can also be uneven (if Ids are issued in steps of 8, say, every element lands in one bucket), and for negative Ids the remainder in C# is negative, so they fall outside 0...7 altogether. For balanced load, prefer Parallel.For with ranges or a Partitioner.

lessons.title: Equality and dictionary keys
lessons.sub: Equals without GetHashCode, and float compared with ==

cards.title: A cabinet with numbered drawers
cards.body:
Dictionary works like a cabinet with numbered drawers. To find a key, it takes two steps:

1. It asks the key for its drawer number (GetHashCode).
2. Inside that drawer, it compares keys for real (Equals).

If two "equal" keys give different numbers, the second one is searched for in the wrong drawer and never found.

cards.title: Equal, but not found
cards.body: The ElementKey class overrides Equals but forgot GetHashCode. By default a class hash is tied to the specific object, not to its contents. Two different objects with identical fields get different numbers.
cards.deep: The contract: if a.Equals(b), the hashes must match. The reverse is not required (hash collisions are allowed). The compiler warns about this (CS0659), and that warning should not be silenced. For classes the default hash is built from object identity (RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode), and it stays the same even when the garbage collector moves the object. "Almost always" because two such hashes occasionally match by chance. A matching bucket is not enough: Dictionary first compares the stored full hash and only then calls Equals.

cards.q: What does this do to GetClashesFor in the service?
options: The cache never hits: every call recomputes everything, and the cache grows
An exception is thrown on first access
The cache returns someone else's clashes
cards.explain: The caller creates a new key object every time, and ContainsKey does not find the "same" one. The query is recomputed and one more entry is added to the dictionary. Memory grows, speed is as if there were no cache.

wrong.1: There is no exception: the dictionary just honestly says "not here".
wrong.2: No foreign data appears, you only lose the cache hit.

cards.task: Find the problems with the dictionary key, the element identifier and the cache.

bugs.title: Equals without GetHashCode
bugs.why: Equal keys land in different dictionary drawers. ContainsKey cannot find them, the cache keeps growing, and every call recomputes everything.

bugs.title: Mutable fields in a key
bugs.why: Once the hash depends on the fields (and it must), changing ElementId after insertion leaves the entry in its old drawer: it can be neither found nor removed. Public fields in a key invite exactly that.

bugs.title: Id ignores ModelId
bugs.why: Elements from different models with the same number are indistinguishable: the a.Id < b.Id check skips their pair, so a clash between them is never found. And if Key is null, you get a NullReferenceException.

bugs.title: Double dictionary lookup
bugs.why: ContainsKey, then the indexer: two lookups instead of one. On a hot path that is wasted work, fixed with TryGetValue.

bugs.title: Cache that is never reset
bugs.why: After clashes are added, removed or imported, the cached lists go stale, and the cache's internal mutable list is handed out to callers.

cards.q: Add the missing method so that equal keys produce the same drawer number.
cards.code:
public override int ___() =>
    HashCode.___(ModelId, ElementId);
cards.explain: HashCode.Combine mixes the field values into one hash. What matters is that the same fields take part as in Equals. In Unity, System.HashCode is available from 2021.2 (the .NET Standard 2.1 profile). On older versions, combine by hand: unchecked((ModelId?.GetHashCode() ?? 0) * 397 ^ ElementId).

cards.q: What happens if you change key.ElementId after dict[key] = value, and the hash is computed from that field?
options: The entry stays in the old drawer and can no longer be found by the key
The dictionary moves the entry to the new drawer itself
An exception is thrown when the field changes
cards.explain: A dictionary computes the hash once, at insertion. It does not watch the key. That is why keys should be immutable: readonly fields, a record or a readonly struct.

wrong.1: The dictionary does not know you changed the field and recomputes nothing.
wrong.2: A plain field can be changed freely, nothing is checked.

cards.q: What is the right way to rewrite the double lookup?
options: if (!_cache.TryGetValue(key, out var list)) _cache[key] = list = Build(key); return list;
return _cache.ContainsKey(key) ? _cache[key] : Build(key);
return _cache[key] ?? Build(key);
cards.explain: TryGetValue searches once and returns the value right away. The second option searches twice and never stores anything in the cache. The third throws KeyNotFoundException when the key is missing.

wrong.1: The lookup is still double, and Build's result is not saved anywhere.
wrong.2: The indexer throws for a missing key, so ?? is never reached.

cards.q: What is -3 % 8 in C#?
cards.code:
int id = -3;
int chunk = id % 8;
cards.explain: In C# the remainder takes the sign of the dividend. So Id % 8 for negative Ids gives a value from -7 to 0, and such elements never land in buckets 0...7. The fix: ((id % 8) + 8) % 8. Do not use Math.Abs: Math.Abs(int.MinValue) throws OverflowException.

wrong.1: That is how mathematicians do it (the remainder is never negative). In C#, the % operator works differently.
wrong.2: The sign cannot vanish: the dividend is negative, so the remainder is too.

cards.title: Fractions are inexact
cards.body:
A computer stores float in binary, and many numbers (even a simple 0.1) cannot be written there exactly. Add 0.1 thirty times and you get 2.9999993, not 3. A == comparison will honestly say "not equal".

You need a tolerance: close enough means equal.
cards.code:
float h = 0f;
for (int i = 0; i < 30; i++) h += 0.1f;   // 2.9999993
h == 3.0f;                       // false
Mathf.Approximately(h, 3.0f);    // true
Math.Abs(h - 3.0f) < 0.001f;     // tolerance in meters
cards.deep: Choose the tolerance for the problem at hand. Mathf.Approximately accepts a difference below 1e-6 of the larger magnitude (plus a tiny absolute floor of Mathf.Epsilon * 8). That is only a few steps of float precision: after a long chain of calculations the error can be larger, and near zero the check becomes almost exact. For heights in meters, an explicit tolerance is safer (for example, 1 mm). Also, NaN == NaN is false, so check for NaN separately.

cards.q: Which properties should a good dictionary key have? Pick all that apply.
options: The fields that Equals and the hash depend on never change
GetHashCode is consistent with Equals
It implements IEquatable<T>, to avoid boxing
The hash is computed from a Name field that the user can rename
cards.explain: Immutability and consistency between Equals and GetHashCode are required. IEquatable<T> removes the cast to object and boxing for structs. A hash over a mutable field breaks lookup.

cards.q: Match each problem with its consequence.
pairs: The cache cannot find its own keys
The entry is lost after an edit
An element "on the level" is not recognized

cards.title: For seniors: a better key
cards.body: In modern .NET the shortest cure is readonly record struct ElementKey(string ModelId, int ElementId). The compiler generates Equals, GetHashCode, IEquatable<T> and the ==/!= operators, the properties become immutable, and the struct creates no garbage as a key.
cards.deep: A caveat for Unity: record needs C# 9, and record struct needs C# 10. Unity from 2021.2 through Unity 6 officially supports C# 9 (check your project's language version), so record struct is not available there, and a record class usually needs an IsExternalInit stub. The safe Unity option is by hand: readonly struct + IEquatable<ElementKey> + GetHashCode + ==/!= operators. If a struct implements neither IEquatable<T> nor an Equals override, the dictionary uses ValueType.Equals: boxing, plus reflection when there are reference fields. And ValueType.GetHashCode may then rely on the first field only, so every key of one model gets the same hash.

lessons.title: Collections and recursion
lessons.sub: Remove inside foreach, an endless tree walk and height comparison

cards.title: The torn-out page
cards.body: You read a list aloud, page after page. Suddenly someone tears out a page while you are reading. You lose your place and do not know what to read next. A foreach over a List behaves the same way and gives up loudly: it throws InvalidOperationException, "Collection was modified".
cards.deep: List<T> has a version counter. Every Add/Remove bumps it, and at the start of each step the enumerator compares its own copy of the version with the current one. A mismatch means an exception. For Dictionary in .NET Core 3.0+, Remove and Clear during enumeration do not bump the version and are therefore allowed. But in .NET Framework and in Unity (the Mono class library, under both Mono and IL2CPP) the dictionary works the old way, and such a loop throws too. Code that "worked" in tests on .NET 8 will crash in Unity.

cards.q: What happens when RemoveResolved runs and the list contains a resolved clash?
options: InvalidOperationException on the next step of the loop
The resolved clashes are quietly removed
All clashes are removed
cards.explain: After Remove, the list version has changed, and the next step of the enumeration notices. Besides, every Remove searches for the item and shifts the tail: that is O(n) per removal.

wrong.1: It would be quiet if you removed outside the loop or used RemoveAll.
wrong.2: The list is not cleared entirely: the loop is simply cut short by an exception.

cards.q: Replace the loop with a single call: remove all resolved items in one pass.
cards.explain: RemoveAll walks the list once, shifts the survivors itself and takes the condition directly. That is O(n) instead of O(n²). Do not forget to reset the cache afterwards, because it still holds stale queries.

cards.q: Which ways safely remove items from List<Clash>? Pick all that apply.
options: _clashes.RemoveAll(c => c.IsResolved)
for (int i = _clashes.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--) with RemoveAt(i)
foreach over _clashes.ToList() calling _clashes.Remove(c)
foreach over _clashes calling _clashes.Remove(c)
cards.explain: RemoveAll is the fastest. A loop from the end does not shift indexes you have not visited yet. A copy via ToList is safe, but costs more time and memory. A direct foreach with Remove crashes.

cards.title: A bottomless nesting doll
cards.body:
CollectFloor calls itself for every child. Each call puts a new plate on a "stack of plates" (the call stack). If the data contains a ring (an element is its own descendant), the plates never run out until the stack collapses.

This crash is called StackOverflowException, and it has a harsh trait: in .NET you cannot catch it with try/catch. The whole process terminates.
cards.deep: A thread's stack is limited (around 1 MB in a typical setup; other platforms and thread pool threads can differ). A depth of tens of thousands of frames can kill the process even without any ring: a very deep tree from an imported model is enough. The C# compiler does not do tail-call optimization, and you cannot rely on the JIT for it either. A Unity caveat: Mono in the Editor sometimes turns the overflow into a regular exception in the console, and the Editor survives. That is no protection: in an IL2CPP build on a device the same error usually means an app crash.

cards.q: Can you wrap the CollectFloor call in try/catch (Exception) and carry on calmly?
options: No: in .NET StackOverflowException cannot be caught, the process dies
Yes, catch (Exception) catches any exception
Yes, but only with catch (StackOverflowException)
cards.explain: Since .NET 2.0, the CLR terminates the process immediately on a stack overflow: carrying on with an exhausted stack is not safe. You have to defend in advance: limit the depth or walk the tree without recursion.

wrong.1: For a stack overflow, no catch block is ever invoked.
wrong.2: That exception type exists, but in .NET no catch clause ever receives it.

cards.task: Three service methods. Each hides its own bug about collections, traversal or numbers. Find all three.

bugs.title: Remove inside foreach
bugs.why: The list changes during enumeration, and the next step throws InvalidOperationException. Also, each removal shifts the tail, so the work is quadratic.

bugs.title: Recursion with no guard against cycles or depth
bugs.why: If Parent and Children form a ring (or the tree is just very deep), the stack overflows. In .NET StackOverflowException cannot be caught: the whole app goes down instead of reporting an error.

bugs.title: float compared with ==
bugs.why: After calculations a height can differ in the last digit. An element that stands on the level is not recognized as such, and the floor looks "empty".

cards.q: Put the steps of an iterative walk (no recursion, protected from rings) in order.
items: Push the root onto a Stack and create a HashSet of visited nodes
While the stack is not empty, pop the top node
If the node was already visited, skip it
Process the node: add it to the result if the floor matches
Push all children of the node onto the stack
cards.explain: The stack replaces function calls, and the visited set breaks rings. The traversal order comes out mirrored for children; if it matters, push children in reverse order.

cards.q: Fill in the walk: "push onto the stack", "pop from the stack" and "remember the visited node".
cards.explain: HashSet.Add returns false if the item was already there. One call both checks and remembers. With Contains, the node would never get into the set.

cards.q: Which level check is the most sensible for heights in meters?
options: Math.Abs(e.Bounds.min.y - levelHeight) < 0.01f
e.Bounds.min.y.Equals(levelHeight)
(int)e.Bounds.min.y == (int)levelHeight
e.Bounds.min.y <= levelHeight
cards.explain: Pick the tolerance by meaning: 1 cm for a building. Equals on a float is the same exact comparison as ==. Casting to int drops the fraction: 2.9999 becomes 2 while 3.0 becomes 3. And <= lets everything below the level through.

wrong.1: It is the same exact comparison as ==. The only difference is NaN: NaN.Equals(NaN) is true, while NaN == NaN is false.
wrong.2: Dropping fractions produces errors of a whole meter.
wrong.3: That checks "not above", not "on the level".

cards.q: Match each symptom with its fix.
pairs: RemoveAll or a copy of the list
The process suddenly exits during a tree walk
Stack and HashSet instead of recursion
A floor looks empty, though it has elements
Removal is slow on thousands of items
One pass instead of Remove in a loop

cards.title: For seniors: what else was forgotten
cards.body: After RemoveResolved (and after Import) the queries in _cache stay old: the clash is already gone from the list, but the cache still returns it. Any change to _clashes must reset the cache, or the cache must store a data version number.
cards.deep: An iterative walk moves the "stack of plates" from the thread stack (around a megabyte) to the heap, where there is far more room. "Visited" marks can also live on the nodes themselves (say, a pass number): no HashSet and no allocations, but two concurrent walks will then get in each other's way. If the tree is edited from another thread, walk an immutable snapshot.

lessons.title: Exceptions and null in Unity
lessons.sub: throw ex, a "dead" GameObject and public fields

cards.title: A letter with a forged return address
cards.body:
An exception carries its call stack: the path it traveled. Think of an envelope with stamps from every post office. When you catch an exception and rethrow it with throw ex;, you paste a new stamp over all the old ones: "sent from here". The real place of failure is lost.

A plain throw; forwards the envelope as it is.
cards.deep: throw ex overwrites the stack trace inside the exception object itself: frames below the catch point disappear. If you need to rethrow a caught exception later or from another place (for example, from a continuation of an async operation) and keep its stack, use ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex).Throw(). If you want to add context, wrap it: throw new ImportException("...", ex), and the original stays in InnerException.

cards.q: What changes in the stack trace if you replace throw ex; with throw;?
options: The frames of the real failure point (inside File.ReadAllText or the parser) show up again
The exception stops being thrown
The stack gets shorter
cards.explain: With throw ex, the trace starts in Import, and everything deeper is gone. With throw; you see the whole chain down to where things really broke. When you debug from a production log, that is the difference between minutes and hours.

wrong.1: The exception is still thrown, only its trace changes.
wrong.2: The opposite: the stack becomes complete, not shorter.

cards.q: Rethrow the exception without losing the stack.
cards.explain: A bare throw; inside catch forwards the same exception with its original stack. throw ex would wipe the stack.

cards.title: Do not catch everything, and do not shout twice
cards.body: Import has three more smells. First: catch (Exception) catches absolutely everything, even what cannot be fixed here. Catch something specific: IOException, JsonException. Second: "log it and rethrow" turns into double (triple) logging at every level. Pick one: either handle it and do not rethrow, or rethrow and do not log, and let whoever makes the decision log it. Third: DeserializeObject can return null (an empty file, or the content "null"), and AddRange(null) throws ArgumentNullException.

cards.q: Check the deserialization result before using it.
cards.explain: If there is no data, a clear error right away beats an ArgumentNullException with a confusing parameter. For ordinary (non-Unity) objects, == null works as expected.

cards.title: Dead, but not empty
cards.body:
A Unity object has two parts: a C# wrapper (what your code sees) and a native object inside the engine. After Destroy, the native part is gone while the wrapper stays, like a nameplate on the door of a demolished room. Unity overloaded the == operator so that such a nameplate compares equal to null ("fake null").

But the ?., ?? and is null operators do not call that overload: they look at the wrapper and see "alive". The result: MissingReferenceException.
cards.deep: Microsoft.Unity.Analyzers warn about this: UNT0007 for ??, UNT0008 for ?., and related rules cover ??= and is null. The rule: for subclasses of UnityEngine.Object, use explicit == null / != null or the implicit conversion to bool. An extra problem in ClashService: the _marker field is private, assigned nowhere, and the class is not a MonoBehaviour, so the Inspector cannot fill it. The method always silently does nothing (the compiler warns with CS0649: the field is never assigned).

cards.q: What does _marker?.SetActive(true) do if the GameObject was already destroyed with Destroy, but the field was not cleared?
options: Throws MissingReferenceException
Quietly skips the call
Creates a new GameObject
cards.explain: The ?. operator only checks the reference to the C# wrapper, and that is not null. So SetActive is called on an object whose native part is already destroyed.

wrong.1: It would skip the call if the check honored the overloaded ==. But ?. does not call it.
wrong.2: Nothing new is created, Unity does not work that way.

cards.task: A part of the service about the data model, import and highlighting. Find as many problems as you can: exceptions, null and class design.

bugs.title: Public mutable Parent and Children
bugs.why: The parent-child link can be broken from either side, even into a ring. And two-way references are a loop for serialization by themselves: Newtonsoft throws "Self referencing loop detected" unless you set ReferenceLoopHandling or serialize separate DTOs.

bugs.title: The _marker field is never assigned
bugs.why: The class is not a MonoBehaviour, so the Inspector will not fill the field. It is always null, and Highlight silently does nothing.

bugs.title: Synchronous file read
bugs.why: File.ReadAllText blocks the thread. If Import is called on Unity's main thread, the game freezes while a large file is read.

bugs.title: Deserialization result is not checked
bugs.why: DeserializeObject returns null for an empty file, and AddRange(null) throws ArgumentNullException. The cache is also not reset after the import.

bugs.title: Too broad catch (Exception)
bugs.why: It catches everything, including what cannot be fixed here. I/O errors and JSON parse errors need specific types.

bugs.title: Logging and then rethrowing
bugs.why: One error gets logged at every level, and the log fills up with duplicates. Also, LogError(ex.Message) writes only the text, with no stack trace (Debug.LogException(ex) would keep it). Log where the error is handled.

bugs.title: throw ex; wipes the stack
bugs.why: The real place of failure vanishes from the trace: only Import is visible. You need throw;.

bugs.title: ?. on a UnityEngine.Object
bugs.why: For a destroyed GameObject, ?. does not see fake null and calls SetActive, which gives MissingReferenceException.

cards.q: Which checks do NOT honor the == overload of UnityEngine.Object and will let a "dead" object through? Pick all that apply.
options: obj?.Method()
obj ?? other
obj is null
obj == null
cards.explain: The ?., ?? and is null operators look at the reference itself and bypass the overload. A plain == null calls Unity's overloaded operator and honestly reports that the object is destroyed.

cards.q: Fix Highlight: use an honest check for a Unity object.
cards.explain: The != operator calls Unity's overload and returns false for a destroyed object. is not null looks similar but bypasses the overload. Also remember to assign the marker field somewhere, in a constructor or via [SerializeField] in a MonoBehaviour.

cards.q: What is the best way to protect the Element tree from Parent and Children getting out of sync?
options: Make the fields private and add an AddChild method that sets Parent itself
Keep the fields public and describe the usage in a comment
Make both fields static
cards.explain: When the only way to change the tree goes through one method, the tree cannot become inconsistent. Expose IReadOnlyList<Element> outward, so nobody can modify the list behind the method's back.

wrong.1: A comment will not stop the mistake, it will happen sooner or later.
wrong.2: static makes the link shared by all elements, which destroys the whole idea.

cards.q: Match each symptom with its cause.
pairs: Only the Import method shows in the log
fake null of a destroyed object
Parent and Children reference each other
Synchronous file read on the main thread

lessons.title: Final: ClashService
lessons.sub: Find the bugs in the full listing

cards.task: This is the whole ClashService sent for review. Mark as many bugs as you can: equality and dictionary, async, threads, collections, recursion, exceptions, Unity null. You need at least 18.

bugs.title: Equals without GetHashCode
bugs.why: Equal keys land in different dictionary drawers, so the cache cannot find its own keys and keeps growing, and every call recomputes everything.

bugs.title: Mutable fields in a key
bugs.why: Once GetHashCode is fixed and depends on the fields, changing a field after insertion "loses" the entry: it can be neither found nor removed.

bugs.title: Id ignores ModelId (and Key may be null)
bugs.why: Elements from different models with the same number are indistinguishable: buckets and comparisons mix them up. A missing Key gives a NullReferenceException.

bugs.title: async void
bugs.why: The caller cannot wait for completion or catch the error. If a task throws, Completed never fires; in Unity the exception only shows up in the console, in .NET without a synchronization context the process crashes.

bugs.title: Closure over the loop variable i
bugs.why: Tasks usually see i == 8, the filter selects nothing, and the service finds zero clashes. The main bug of the listing.

bugs.title: Splitting by Id % 8 breaks the pairs
bugs.why: Elements from different buckets are never compared, so some clashes can never be found. Negative Ids give a negative remainder.

bugs.title: Lazy Where enumerated many times
bugs.why: The inner loop re-runs the filter for every outer element: n² predicate calls and repeated computation of the source.

bugs.title: Race on List.Add
bugs.why: List<T> is not thread-safe: writing from eight threads loses items and throws exceptions.

bugs.title: Non-atomic counter with a misleading name
bugs.why: _processed++ from several threads loses increments (Interlocked is needed), and the name promises "processed" while it counts clashes.

bugs.title: a.Id < b.Id drops pairs with equal Ids
bugs.why: Elements from different models with the same ElementId are never compared, so a clash between them is never found.

bugs.title: Remove inside foreach
bugs.why: The list changes during enumeration: InvalidOperationException on the next step. Plus quadratic work. Use RemoveAll.

bugs.title: Double dictionary lookup
bugs.why: ContainsKey, then the indexer: two lookups instead of one. Fixed with TryGetValue.

bugs.title: Cache is never reset and exposes its internal list
bugs.why: After removal, import and new clashes the cache holds stale queries, and a mutable internal list is handed out.

bugs.title: Recursion with no guard against rings or depth
bugs.why: A ring in Parent/Children or a very deep tree causes StackOverflowException. In .NET it cannot be caught and the process ends; in an IL2CPP build the app crashes.

bugs.title: float compared with ==
bugs.why: Heights are inexact in the last digits, so an element on the level is not recognized as such. A tolerance is needed.

bugs.title: throw ex; wipes the stack
bugs.why: Only Import remains in the trace, and the real place of failure vanishes. You need throw;.

bugs.title: Logging and then rethrowing
bugs.why: The same error gets logged at every level, and the log fills up with duplicates. And LogError(ex.Message) drops the stack trace: use Debug.LogException(ex) where the error is handled.

bugs.title: Too broad catch (Exception)
bugs.why: It catches everything, even what cannot be fixed here. Use specific types (IOException, JsonException).

bugs.title: DeserializeObject can return null
bugs.why: For an empty file or the content "null", AddRange(null) throws ArgumentNullException. The cache is not reset after the import, and every clash from the JSON gets its own copies of Element, unrelated to the model's elements.

bugs.title: Synchronous file read
bugs.why: File.ReadAllText blocks the thread. On Unity's main thread the game freezes while the file is read.

bugs.title: ?. on a UnityEngine.Object
bugs.why: For a destroyed GameObject (fake null), ?. does not work as a check and gives MissingReferenceException.

bugs.title: The _marker field is never assigned
bugs.why: The class is not a MonoBehaviour, so the Inspector will not fill the field. It is always null, and Highlight silently does nothing.

bugs.title: Public mutable Parent and Children
bugs.why: The link can be broken from either side, even into a ring. And two-way references are a loop for serialization: Newtonsoft throws "Self referencing loop detected".

cards.q: Which bug is the main one, the reason the service "silently finds zero clashes"?
options: Closure over the loop variable i in Task.Run
async void in RunAsync
float compared with ==
cards.explain: All tasks see i == 8, and the filter Id % 8 == 8 lets no element through. The other bugs break the result less often or loudly, while this one empties it without a single error.

wrong.1: async void hides exceptions, but it does not blank the result.
wrong.2: float == breaks the level check, not the clash search.

cards.q: Which bugs in the listing show up "intermittently", not on every run? Pick all that apply.
options: _processed++ from several threads
_clashes.Add from several threads
Closure over i (depends on when the tasks start)
Remove inside foreach in RemoveResolved
cards.explain: Races and the closure depend on timing. Remove inside foreach fails every time there is something to remove: that error is deterministic.

cards.q: Which of these errors in the listing cannot be caught with try/catch?
options: StackOverflowException from CollectFloor
InvalidOperationException from RemoveResolved
ArgumentNullException from Import
MissingReferenceException from Highlight
cards.explain: In .NET a stack overflow ends the process immediately, and no catch runs. The other three are ordinary exceptions and can be caught. So the guard against rings must be in the code up front.

cards.q: Put the steps of a Dictionary key lookup in order.
items: Call GetHashCode on the key
Pick a drawer (bucket) by the hash
Walk the entries of that drawer
For entries with the same hash, compare keys with Equals
Return the found value
cards.explain: If equal keys have different GetHashCode values, step 2 leads to another drawer, and even if the drawer matches, the stored hash does not. Equals is never reached.

cards.q: Fix the launcher: the right return type and a list materialized once.
cards.explain: Instead of async void you need async Task, so callers can await and catch errors. ToList() pins the data once, and tasks do not recompute a lazy query. Where materializes nothing by itself.

cards.q: Which line erases the real call stack of the exception?
cards.explain: The throw ex; line restarts the trace at the current place. The correct form is throw;. The logging above does not erase the stack, but it makes the error "noisy".

cards.q: Match each bug with its symptom.
pairs: The cache cannot find its own keys
The process dies, catch does not help

cards.q: What is the best way to redo ElementKey?
options: An immutable struct: readonly struct with IEquatable, GetHashCode and == (or a readonly record struct)
Keep the class and write GetHashCode over the mutable fields
Use a string of ModelId + ElementId concatenated on every call
