cards.explain: A key must be immutable, with Equals and GetHashCode consistent; a struct with IEquatable<T> creates no garbage and is not boxed. In .NET with C# 10, a readonly record struct generates all of this, while in Unity (C# 9) you write such a struct by hand.

wrong.1: A hash over mutable fields loses entries after an edit.
wrong.2: Concatenating a string on every call creates garbage, and the key stays flimsy.

units.title: Task 3: TileLoader
units.blurb: Blocking inside async, a deadlock on Unity’s main thread, races and GetOrAdd, a timer the GC collects, and a tidy-looking cancellation that cancels nothing.

lessons.title: Blocking inside async
lessons.sub: Wait, Sleep and the Unity context deadlock

cards.title: A ticket office with four windows
cards.body:
A map tile loader downloads small pieces of a map. To avoid flooding the server, it lets at most four tiles download at once. Think of a ticket office with four windows: the fifth person waits until a window frees up.

In C# this "office" is a SemaphoreSlim(4). You take a spot with Wait and give it back with Release. You are reviewing a method that uses it inside async. It has three problems at once.

cards.title: async does not mean "on another thread"
cards.body:
An async method runs as plain code on the caller's thread, right up to the first await that has not already finished. Only there does the method step aside and release the thread.

So everything before the first await, including a blocking Wait(), runs on whichever thread called the method. If the method is called from a GetOrAdd factory, the factory runs on that same thread too.

cards.q: Game code on the Unity main thread calls GetTileAsync(7, ct). All 4 semaphore spots are taken. Which thread will block in _throttle.Wait()?
options: The Unity main thread: it made the call
A thread-pool thread: async always moves to the pool
A new thread created by the semaphore
cards.explain: Until the first unfinished await, the method runs synchronously on the caller's thread. The GetOrAdd factory is also called synchronously. So Wait() blocks the main thread and the game freezes.

wrong.1: async by itself moves nothing to the pool. That is what Task.Run does.

cards.title: The deadlock through the Unity context
cards.body:
The Unity main thread has its own SynchronizationContext. An await that starts on the main thread captures that context, and the continuation is queued back to the main thread. Unity drains that queue once per frame, in its player loop.

Now the picture: four loads hold the spots, and their continuations (where Release lives) wait for the main thread. The main thread is stuck in Wait(), waiting for a spot to free up. Each waits for the other. That is a deadlock.
cards.deep: The context is captured only if SynchronizationContext.Current is not null where the await runs. In Unity that is the main thread. If the four loads holding the spots started on a pool thread, their continuations run in the pool, Release happens, and the main thread only stalls until a spot frees up. That is why the bug comes and goes: it depends on which thread started the loads that hold the spots.

cards.q: Put the deadlock steps in order.
items: Four loads take all semaphore spots and wait for the network
The main thread calls GetTileAsync and blocks in Wait(): no spots left
A network reply arrives; the continuation (with Release) is queued to the main thread
The main thread never drains its queue: it is blocked in Wait()
Release never runs, no spot is freed, Wait never wakes up
cards.explain: A closed loop: the main thread waits for Release, and only the main thread can run Release.

cards.task: Find three problems: a blocked thread, a spot that may never be released, and a needless thread stall. Tap the lines, then press Check.

bugs.title: Synchronous Wait() in an async method
bugs.why: It blocks the calling thread. On the Unity main thread that freezes the game and deadlocks: the continuations that call Release are waiting for this very thread.

bugs.title: Thread.Sleep in an async method
bugs.why: It blocks the whole thread. The continuation after await came back to the Unity main thread, so the frame stalls for 50 ms per tile. Use await Task.Delay(50, ct): it holds no thread.

bugs.title: Release outside try/finally
bugs.why: If the network or Parse throws, the code never reaches Release. After four such errors all spots are lost for good and every load hangs.

cards.title: The spot nobody returned
cards.body:
Picture a cloakroom with 4 hooks. A person hangs a coat, trips on the way out and never comes back. That hook is taken forever. After four such people the cloakroom is closed to everyone.

That is Release without finally. One network error and a spot is gone. _pending is not decremented either, so _allLoaded never fires. A single failure shuts down the whole loader, and with no message in the log: loads just "hang".
cards.deep: One detail when fixing it: open the try after the spot is acquired. If WaitAsync(ct) throws OperationCanceledException (cancellation), the finally must not call Release: you never took a spot, and the semaphore count would grow above the original 4.

cards.q: The loader has no try/finally. Four loads in a row fail (the server returns errors). What happens to a fifth, perfectly healthy load?
options: It hangs waiting for a spot: all 4 spots are lost
It works; the semaphore recovers by itself
It throws immediately
cards.explain: A semaphore only remembers how many spots are free. A load that failed never returned its spot, and the semaphore does not know. After four losses there are zero free spots, permanently.

wrong.1: SemaphoreSlim does not track who took what. It cannot recover on its own.

cards.q: Build the correct "ticket office": it waits without blocking and returns the spot in every case.
cards.explain: WaitAsync holds no thread and Task.Delay does not block one. finally runs on success and on error, and the Release inside it returns the spot.

cards.q: What is true about ConfigureAwait(false) in this loader?
options: The continuation after await usually runs on the thread pool, not the Unity main thread
The heavy Tile.Parse then no longer slows down frames
Right after it you can safely touch Unity scene objects
By itself it removes the blocking Wait()
cards.explain: ConfigureAwait(false) means "do not return to the captured context", so parsing leaves the main thread. You must not touch Unity API after it. It does not remove Wait(), which runs before the first await. It does break the deadlock loop, though: Release runs on the pool and wakes the main thread, although the game still freezes until then.

cards.q: Match the symptom to its cause.
pairs: A frame hitches after every downloaded tile
Thread.Sleep in a continuation on the main thread
After a few network errors no tiles load at all
The game hangs forever while the CPU sits idle
Deadlock: the continuation with Release waits for the blocked main thread
The deadlock is gone after ConfigureAwait(false), but the game still stalls at times
Wait() before the first await still blocks the main thread

lessons.title: Shared state and races
lessons.sub: GetOrAdd, counters, Dictionary and the stop flag

cards.title: One notebook for everyone
cards.body:
Imagine a single notebook shared by everybody. While one person writes a number, another is already reading that line, and a third is erasing the line next to it. The result is a mess. That is a data race: the outcome depends on who got there first.

The loader has four shared "notebooks": the task map _loading, the finished-tile map _loaded, the counter _pending and the flag _stopRequested. Each one is handled carelessly.

For example, a Dictionary is safe if it is only read. But reading while another thread writes is not allowed: you can get garbage or an exception.

cards.title: GetOrAdd: "one value" does not mean "one factory call"
cards.body:
ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd(key, factory) guarantees that the dictionary ends up with one value for the key. But the factory is not under a lock. If two threads both miss the key at the same time, both call the factory. One result wins and the other is simply thrown away.

For a harmless factory ("create an object") that is fine. But our factory calls LoadAsync, which has already started: it took a semaphore spot, incremented _pending and went to the network. The discarded Task is not cancelled; it keeps running. The tile is downloaded twice.

cards.q: What is true about ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd(key, valueFactory)?
options: There will be one value for the key, but valueFactory may run on several threads
valueFactory runs under a lock, exactly once per key
valueFactory is always called twice
If the factory is slow, the dictionary blocks for all keys
cards.explain: The documentation says it: the factory runs outside the dictionary's internal locks, so it can run in parallel, and only one value is stored. The other results are discarded.

wrong.1: That is exactly what GetOrAdd does not promise. If you need exactly one run, wrap the value in Lazy.

cards.title: The fix: Lazy
cards.body: Put a recipe in the dictionary instead of a running task: a Lazy<Task<Tile>>. You can create as many recipes as you like; they start nothing. The work starts on the first access to .Value, and by default Lazy guarantees the recipe runs once.
cards.deep: The default mode of Lazy<T> is ExecutionAndPublication: the factory runs once under a lock. But .Value starts LoadAsync right away on the caller's thread (until the first await), so the blocking Wait() from lesson 1 still has to go. And Lazy does not stop failures from being cached: an async method does not throw to the caller, the error goes into the Task, and Lazy keeps the failed task forever (more on that below).

cards.q: Complete GetTileAsync so that each tile is loaded exactly once.
cards.explain: Lazy delays the start of LoadAsync until .Value is read and makes sure it starts once. The Lazy wrapper that lost the GetOrAdd race is never unwrapped, so it starts nothing.

cards.task: Find four problems with state shared between threads. Tap the lines, then press Check.

bugs.title: Non-atomic counter and SetResult
bugs.why: --_pending loses updates under a race, and the count can hit zero between two tiles: waiters think everything is loaded. A second SetResult throws InvalidOperationException.

bugs.title: GetOrAdd with a side effect in the factory
bugs.why: The factory can run on two threads at once: the tile loads twice and _pending and the semaphore are touched twice. Use Lazy<Task<Tile>>.

bugs.title: Reading a Dictionary without a lock
bugs.why: Other threads write to _loaded under a lock, but this code reads without one. Reading during a write gives garbage or an exception.

bugs.title: Stop flag without synchronization
bugs.why: Under the memory model, a plain bool shared across threads does not guarantee the loop will see the write: the JIT may read it once. Here the lock in Compact and the await save you by accident; a CancellationToken is the reliable way (volatile at the very least).

cards.title: The counter that hit zero at the wrong time
cards.body:
A scenario. Tiles A-D hold all four spots, _pending = 4, and tile E waits at the semaphore. A calls Release, E wakes up but has not reached Increment yet. Meanwhile A-D bring the counter down to 0 and announce: "everything is loaded!". The announcement came too early. Even simpler: the game requests tiles in waves, and the counter hits zero between waves.

When E finishes, the counter hits 0 again, and a second SetResult throws InvalidOperationException. That happens after Release: a tile that loaded fine returns an error, and the failed task stays in the cache. The fix: count at the point where work appears (in GetTileAsync), use Interlocked, and complete with TrySetResult.
cards.deep: One more subtlety: a TaskCompletionSource created without TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously runs the waiters' continuations synchronously inside SetResult. So foreign code after await WhenAllLoaded() starts running on the loading thread, inside our LoadAsync, and in general under whatever locks the caller of SetResult holds. That is why a TCS is almost always created with this flag.

cards.q: Put in order the events that make the counter hit zero too early.
items: Tiles A-D hold all 4 spots, _pending = 4, tile E waits at the semaphore
A calls Release, E wakes up but has not run Increment yet
A-D bring the counter to 0, SetResult(true): "all done"
E increments the counter, loads, brings it back to 0, and the second SetResult throws
cards.explain: The counter only counts loads that passed the semaphore, not loads that were already requested. So zero is possible while work still remains.

cards.q: Which fix for _pending and _allLoaded is the most reliable?
options: Interlocked.Increment when a tile is queued, Interlocked.Decrement in finally, complete with TrySetResult
Replace --_pending with _pending -= 1
Declare _pending volatile and keep --_pending
Wrap SetResult in try/catch and swallow the exception
cards.explain: You need three things together: count at the right moment (when work appears), do it atomically, and survive a repeated completion.

wrong.1: That is the same non-atomic code in different words.
wrong.2: volatile gives visibility, not atomicity: --_pending is still a read, a subtract and a write.

cards.title: A failed task stays in the dictionary
cards.body:
While a Task sits in _loading, every later GetTileAsync(id) receives that same Task. If it ended with an error (or was cancelled), it stays that way. The network drops for one second and the tile is now "broken" until restart: nobody retries.

Failed entries must be removed. Cache success, not failure.
cards.deep: A subtlety: if the error happens synchronously, before GetOrAdd returns and the entry is in the dictionary, TryRemove does nothing, and the entry is added afterwards anyway. It is safer to remove in a continuation outside, once the task is already in the dictionary. Remove this exact task, not "whatever is under the key", or you may throw out a newer, successful attempt (in .NET 5+ use TryRemove(KeyValuePair); before that, ICollection<KeyValuePair>.Remove). Be careful with cancellation too: a task cancelled by someone else's token must not stay in the cache forever either.

cards.q: The tile server answered 503 for tile 42, then recovered. The player requests tile 42 again. What does the original loader return?
options: The same failed Task: the error was cached
A fresh, successful load
null
cards.explain: The dictionary stores a Task per key and never replaces it. Later calls get the same failed task until the entry is removed.

cards.q: Which of these is a data race in the loader?
options: Reading _loaded.Count in the timer while another thread writes under a lock
Two threads calling GetOrAdd for different keys at the same time
A bool _stopRequested written on one thread and read in another thread's loop
Reading the id variable inside the factory lambda
cards.explain: The first and the third: shared data, one thread writes, the other has no synchronization. ConcurrentDictionary is designed to be thread-safe for different keys, and id is a local, immutable parameter.

lessons.title: Timers, background tasks, cancellation
lessons.sub: Timer and the GC, StartNew(async), the decoy token

cards.title: An alarm clock with no owner
cards.body:
You set an alarm clock and hide it in a drawer nobody knows about. Two outcomes are possible: the cleaner throws the drawer out and the alarm goes silent, or it rings forever and nobody can switch it off.

That is exactly what the loader constructor does: var timer = new Timer(…). The variable is local, and nothing else references the timer. In .NET (Framework and modern) the garbage collector may collect it, and the progress bar stops updating "at some random moment", with no error. In Mono, which Unity runs on, the scheduler itself holds active timers, so the timer does not die, but nothing can stop it either: it keeps calling ReportProgress even after a scene change. Both outcomes are bad.

cards.q: What does the .NET documentation say about a System.Threading.Timer that nothing references any more?
options: The GC may collect it and the callback stops: keep a reference for as long as you need the timer
The timer keeps running until Dispose is called, in every implementation
The GC collects it exactly when the constructor returns
The callback of such a timer moves to the main thread
cards.explain: The documentation explicitly says to keep a reference to the Timer. When exactly it gets collected depends on when a garbage collection happens. In Mono (Unity) the scheduler holds active timers, but that is an implementation detail, not a promise, and such a timer still cannot be stopped.

wrong.1: That is how Mono behaves, but the .NET documentation does not promise it: in .NET Framework and modern .NET an unreferenced timer is collected.
wrong.2: Collection timing is not deterministic: the object becomes unreachable, but it is collected at some later garbage collection.

cards.title: What else is wrong with the timer
cards.body:
A Timer callback runs on a thread-pool thread, not on the main thread. Yet it writes _progressBar.value, which calls Unity API. That is only allowed on the main thread.

Also: dueTime = 0 fires the first call immediately, in parallel with the rest of the constructor. That is harmless here, but the callback may see any field assigned after the timer is created as still empty. And after a scene change the Slider is destroyed while the timer (if alive) keeps writing to it.

The right way: keep the timer in a field, call Dispose when stopping, and simply store the progress value in a field that Update reads on the main thread.
cards.deep: In Unity, writing to a UI object from the pool often "just does not crash", and sometimes throws UnityException ("can only be called from the main thread"): it depends on the specific API and version. So the rule is strict: do not touch Unity API from background threads; hand results to the main thread (through a field plus Update, or through a captured UnitySynchronizationContext). About the GC: in .NET an unreferenced timer is stopped at some garbage collection (its finalizer shuts it down), so it "lives" for a random time. In Mono (and IL2CPP, which uses the same class libraries) an active timer sits in a static scheduler list and is not collected. Rely on neither.

cards.q: Fix the timer: keep it in a field and dispose it.
cards.explain: The field keeps the timer alive as long as the loader lives. Dispose stops it and frees its resources. (In real code the callback also must not touch the Slider directly.)

cards.title: Task.Factory.StartNew(async …) is a "Task in a Task"
cards.body:
An async lambda returns a Task. StartNew wraps that result in one more task, so you get a Task<Task>. The outer task counts as finished as soon as the lambda reaches its first await, which is almost immediately.

The inner task (the loop with Compact) lives on its own. If an exception happens in it, nobody sees it: nobody watches the inner task. The fix is one word: Task.Run unwraps the nested task automatically.
cards.deep: The second StartNew trap: without an explicit scheduler it uses TaskScheduler.Current, not the pool. Call it from inside a task running on a custom scheduler (say, a "main-thread scheduler") and the background work lands there too. Task.Run is StartNew with TaskScheduler.Default, DenyChildAttach and an automatic Unwrap.

cards.q: What type does Task.Factory.StartNew(async () => { … }) return without Unwrap?
options: Task<Task>
Task
void
Task<T> for the T in the lambda body
cards.explain: StartNew runs the delegate and wraps its result in a Task. The result of an async lambda is itself a Task, so the type is nested. Task.Run or .Unwrap() turn it into a plain Task.

cards.task: Find four problems in the constructor, the preload and the background loop. Tap the lines, then press Check.

bugs.title: Timer in a local variable
bugs.why: Nothing references the timer: in .NET the GC collects it and progress quietly freezes, while in Mono (Unity) it cannot be stopped at all. Use a field and Dispose.

bugs.title: Fire-and-forget in PreloadAll
bugs.why: The returned Tasks are ignored: errors go unobserved and nobody can wait for the result. And the factory with its blocking Wait() runs right inside this loop: from the fifth id on, PreloadAll blocks the calling thread.

bugs.title: CancellationToken.None instead of a token
bugs.why: It looks like a neatly passed token, but cancellation is switched off completely: nobody can stop the load from outside.

bugs.title: StartNew(async) and Delay without a token
bugs.why: You get a Task<Task> and exceptions in the loop are lost. And Task.Delay(1000) without ct is not interrupted on stop and holds the loop until the pause ends.

cards.title: A token that only looks like cancellation
cards.body:
The method takes a CancellationToken ct and then never uses it: not in GetByteArrayAsync, not in Delay. It is an "exit" sign above a locked door. And PreloadAll passes CancellationToken.None, a token that can never be cancelled.

One more trap. Everyone who asks for the same tile shares one task. The factory closes over the ct of the first caller. If that caller cancels, the cancellation hits everyone else too.
cards.deep: The usual scheme: the shared work gets the loader's own token (a CancellationTokenSource on the object), and each caller cancels only its own wait with task.WaitAsync(ct) (available in .NET 6+) or Task.WhenAny with a cancellation task. A version caveat: Task.WaitAsync and the HttpClient.GetByteArrayAsync(url, ct) overload only arrived in .NET 6 and .NET 5. Unity (the .NET Standard 2.1 and .NET Framework profiles) has neither: pass the token through GetAsync(url, ct) or SendAsync(request, ct), and build a cancellable wait with Task.WhenAny.

cards.q: The token is passed everywhere except one line. Tap it.
cards.explain: GetAsync(url) without a token: cancellation will not interrupt the network request, which runs to the end. It should be Http.GetAsync(url, ct).

cards.title: PreloadAll: fire and forget
cards.body:
The loop calls GetTileAsync and throws the task away. An exception inside such a task is never seen, and you cannot tell when everything is ready.

Worse, the "fire and forget" is an illusion. The factory and Wait() run synchronously, right inside this loop. From the fifth id on, the loop blocks in Wait() until a spot frees up, and PreloadAll turns into a long blocking call. On the Unity main thread that is the deadlock from lesson 1. And if hundreds of pool tasks call GetTileAsync at once, every waiter holds a whole thread: the pool starves and even unrelated tasks start to lag.

The fix: return a Task, wait with await, and let an asynchronous WaitAsync inside the load enforce the "at most 4" limit.

cards.q: What makes PreloadAllAsync from the example better than PreloadAll that ignores the tasks?
options: It returns a Task: you can await completion, see exceptions and pass a token
It loads tiles faster because it uses more threads
It replaces the semaphore, so no limiter is needed
cards.explain: The tasks are gathered in WhenAll, so exceptions and completion are observable. Speed and threads have nothing to do with it, and the limiter is still needed, just a non-blocking one.

wrong.2: Task.WhenAll limits nothing: the limit still comes from WaitAsync inside the load.

cards.q: What is true about background tasks and timers in this loader?
options: A System.Threading.Timer callback runs on a thread-pool thread, not the Unity main thread
Task.Run unwraps an async lambda, while StartNew(async) does not
An ignored Task guarantees that exceptions are shown in the Unity console
A CancellationToken is a better way to stop a background loop than a flag
cards.explain: The first, second and fourth are true. An ignored task does the opposite: it hides exceptions. At best they surface in the TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException event once the GC gets to the task.

lessons.title: Final: the whole TileLoader
lessons.sub: Find every bug in the tile loader

cards.title: The exit review
cards.body:
Here is the whole tile loader. You have seen it in pieces: blocking, races, timers and cancellation. Now find everything yourself. There are more than ten bugs, and they are linked: one hides another.

A hint on the order: first scan the threads (who runs which line), then the shared data (who writes and who reads), then the lifetimes (who holds a reference, who will stop what).

cards.task: Find all bugs in TileLoader. Tap the problem lines, then press Check. There are 12 in total.

bugs.title: Synchronous Wait() in an async method
bugs.why: The GetOrAdd factory runs on the caller's thread. On the Unity main thread that means a freeze and a deadlock: Release sits in a continuation that Unity posts back to the same blocked thread. Use await _throttle.WaitAsync(ct).

bugs.title: Release and counter outside try/finally
bugs.why: Any network or Parse error leaves the spot taken. After four errors the semaphore is exhausted for good, and _pending is not decremented, so _allLoaded never fires.

bugs.title: Thread.Sleep in an async method
bugs.why: It blocks a thread: the continuation after await came back to the Unity main thread, so the frame stalls. Use await Task.Delay(50, ct). The continuations should also leave the main thread via ConfigureAwait(false).

bugs.title: The token is never used, and PreloadAll passes None
bugs.why: GetByteArrayAsync is called without a token, and None disables cancellation entirely. Besides, the factory captures the first caller's token, so their cancellation hits everyone sharing the task.

bugs.title: Non-atomic counter and TCS
bugs.why: --_pending loses updates, and zero is possible between tiles, so "all loaded" fires too early. A second SetResult throws. Use Interlocked, TrySetResult and RunContinuationsAsynchronously.

bugs.title: GetOrAdd starts LoadAsync in the factory
bugs.why: The factory may run on two threads: the tile loads twice and the counter and semaphore are hit twice. Store a Lazy<Task<Tile>>.

bugs.title: Failed tasks stay in the cache forever
bugs.why: A repeated GetTileAsync returns the same failed or cancelled Task, with no retry. Failed entries must be removed.

bugs.title: Reading _loaded without a lock
bugs.why: Other threads write to the Dictionary under a lock, while TryGetLoaded and ReportProgress read it without one. A read during a write yields garbage or an exception.

bugs.title: Timer in a local variable
bugs.why: Nothing references the timer: in .NET the GC collects it and progress quietly freezes; in Mono (Unity) it cannot be stopped. Also the callback runs on the pool and writes to the Slider, while Unity API is main-thread only.

bugs.title: StartNew(async) and Delay without a token
bugs.why: You get a Task<Task> and loop exceptions are lost. Task.Delay(1000) is not interrupted by Stop(). Use Task.Run and a token.

bugs.title: Stop flag without synchronization
bugs.why: A plain bool across threads formally does not guarantee the loop sees the write, and Stop() does not wait for the loop to end. Use a CancellationTokenSource.

bugs.title: PreloadAll: fire-and-forget
bugs.why: The tasks are discarded: errors are invisible and nobody can wait. And the factory with Wait() runs right in the loop: from the fifth id on, PreloadAll blocks the calling thread (on the main thread, a deadlock). Return a Task instead.

cards.q: When does the Wait() in LoadAsync cause a deadlock?
options: GetTileAsync is called from the Unity main thread while all 4 spots are taken
Only if the call comes from a thread-pool thread
Only if the tile server is unreachable
On any call, even when spots are free
cards.explain: Wait() has to really block (no free spots) and block the main thread that Unity will post the Release continuations to (which happens if the loads holding the spots also started on the main thread). While spots are free, Wait passes instantly.

wrong.3: With a free spot Wait() returns at once; nothing blocks.

cards.q: Which changes in LoadAsync are actually needed?
options: await _throttle.WaitAsync(ct) instead of Wait()
Release and the counter decrement in finally
Replace lock (_sync) with a Mutex
await Task.Delay(50, ct) instead of Thread.Sleep(50)
cards.explain: The lock around the dictionary write is fine here and short. A Mutex is heavier, thread-affine and fixes nothing. The other three changes remove the blocking and the lost spot.

cards.q: Replace the stop flag with a token: complete the background loop.
cards.explain: Task.Run unwraps the async lambda, and Cancel signals both the loop and the Delay. Task.Delay throws on cancellation, so in real code you catch OperationCanceledException.

cards.q: Put the correct LoadAsync outline in order.
items: await _throttle.WaitAsync(ct): wait for a spot without blocking
try {
Download and parse the tile, passing ct
Write the result into _loaded under a lock
} finally { Release; Interlocked.Decrement }
cards.explain: Take the spot before the try (otherwise a cancelled wait would release a spot we never took) and give it back in finally in every case.

cards.q: Match each bug to its consequence.
pairs: After four errors every load hangs
The Timer callback writes to the Slider
Unity API is called off the main thread
Errors in the background loop are lost
GetOrAdd starting work in the factory

cards.q: A player reports: after a few network failures the map stops loading even though the network is back, and the game does not lag. What is the most likely cause?
options: The semaphore spot is not returned on error (no finally)
The Timer was collected by the GC
Thread.Sleep freezes the main thread
ConfigureAwait(false) is missing
cards.explain: The symptom "quietly stopped loading after errors, no lag" is an exhausted semaphore. A frozen main thread would show as lag, and a Timer problem would only affect the progress bar (and in Unity's Mono runtime an unreferenced timer is not even collected).

units.blurb: Allocations in Update, leaked materials and broken batching, OnEnable without OnDisable, HasFlag, a comparator that throws, and a cache that is LRU in name only.

lessons.title: Allocations in Update
lessons.sub: LINQ, GetComponent, strings and WaitForSeconds every frame

cards.title: A pile of trash every frame
cards.body:
Picture a kitchen where the cook drops a wrapper on the floor after every dish. A few dishes, nobody notices. But every so often a cleaner walks in and stops the whole kitchen for a moment. That cleaner is the garbage collector (GC).

A game draws 60 frames a second, so a frame has only about 16 ms. If Update creates new objects every frame (lists, strings, delegates), garbage piles up and the cleaner arrives in the middle of a frame. The game stutters.

In this lesson you hunt through ClashMarkers.Update for anything that makes garbage or does expensive work every frame.
cards.deep: Unity uses the Boehm collector: it is non-generational and does not compact the heap. The incremental GC (an option since Unity 2019.1) spreads the pause over several frames, but it does not remove the cost of the allocations or of heap scanning. So when you review a hot path (Update, physics, short-step coroutines) the goal is zero allocations in steady state.

cards.task: This method runs every frame. Flag the lines that allocate or do needlessly expensive work every frame (the .material line is the topic of the next lesson, but it is a bug too).

bugs.title: LINQ chain in Update
bugs.why: Every frame, Where, OrderBy and ToList create iterator objects, sort buffers and a new list with its array. That is steady garbage and regular GC pauses.

bugs.title: Camera.main and Distance (with a square root) inside the sort key
bugs.why: The key is computed for every marker every frame, and each time it reads Camera.main (a tag lookup in old Unity versions). Distance also does a square root. Read the camera position once and compare squared distances.

bugs.title: GetComponent for every marker every frame
bugs.why: A component lookup is not free. With hundreds of markers it eats a visible share of the frame. Cache the reference when the marker is created.

bugs.title: renderer.material makes a copy of the material
bugs.why: The first access clones the material for this renderer: leaked copies and broken batching. The materials lesson covers it in detail.

bugs.title: String and TextMesh work every frame
bugs.why: Concatenation creates a new string per marker per frame, and assigning text every frame pushes the string into the native TextMesh, which may rebuild its mesh even though the text is the same. Plus one more expensive GetComponentInChildren.

cards.title: What LINQ really does
cards.body:
LINQ looks like one line, but a whole workshop runs underneath:

Where creates an iterator object and holds a delegate. OrderBy copies all elements into a buffer, computes a key for each one and keeps an array of keys. ToList allocates a new list and its backing array.

Once, while loading a level, that is fine. Every frame it means dozens of small objects for the GC to clean up.

The replacement: a reusable List field (Clear() and refill in a plain loop) and an in-place sort.
cards.deep:
The compiler (Roslyn) caches a lambda that captures nothing in a static field. Neither lambda in this Update captures anything (Camera.main is a static property), so the garbage here comes from the iterators, the OrderBy buffer and the list, not from delegates. A lambda that does capture something (say, a local camera position) allocates a closure object and a new delegate on every call of the method. So list.Sort((a, b) => …) with a captured local allocates too. In the hottest code, keep the camera position in a field and precompute squared distances into a parallel array.

One more detail: OrderBy computes the key once per element, not once per comparison, so Camera.main is read n times here, not n log n. Still n times too many.

cards.q: There are 200 markers and the list must be ordered by distance to the camera every frame. What is best?
options: Keep the LINQ and wrap it in try/catch
Keep a list field, refill it without LINQ, compare squared distances, and skip the sort when the camera barely moved
Run the LINQ on a background thread with Task.Run
Call GC.Collect() at the end of Update
cards.explain: Remove the cause of the garbage and the extra work. Do not hide it.

wrong.2: You may touch Transform and GameObject only from the main thread, and the garbage would not disappear anyway.
wrong.3: Forcing a collection every frame causes huge pauses on its own.

cards.title: Cache it: once instead of a thousand times
cards.body:
A good reviewer asks about every line in Update: "Could we compute this earlier?"

GetComponent, GetComponentInChildren, Camera.main, Find…: fetch them once in Awake or when the marker is created, and keep them in a field. Prebuild the labels "Clash 1", "Clash 2"… in an array and assign them only when the value has changed.

You do not need the root to compare distances: sqrMagnitude goes up and down exactly like the distance.
cards.deep: Since Unity 2020.2, Camera.main is cached inside the engine and is cheap. In older versions it was a FindGameObjectWithTag on every call. Do not rely on that in code that builds on several versions. Caching is still better, because it also makes the "no camera" case (null) visible.

cards.q: Let us finish the cache: when a marker is created, fetch its renderer and text once. Fill in the blanks.
cards.explain: The renderer sits on the marker itself and the text on a child object. Do the expensive lookup once at registration, then use the ready struct in Update.

cards.q: A coroutine waits 0.05 seconds in a loop. Remove the allocation on every iteration.
cards.explain: WaitForSeconds is a plain class, so new in a loop makes garbage 20 times a second. One shared instance is safe to reuse.

cards.q: The method is called with a plain List<ClashScore>. What allocates here?
options: Nothing: the List<T> enumerator is a struct
The enumerator gets boxed into an object: foreach goes through the interface and calls IEnumerable<T>.GetEnumerator()
All the list elements are copied
cards.explain: A direct foreach over a List<T> does not allocate, because the compiler uses the struct enumerator. Through the IList<T> interface it becomes a boxed object, and you get garbage on every call.

wrong.0: That is true only for a foreach over a variable of type List<T>. Here the type is an interface.
wrong.2: Nothing is copied. Only the enumerator is allocated.

cards.q: Which line creates garbage on every Update call?
cards.explain: new List<...>() is a heap object that lives for one frame. Vector3 and float are structs that live on the stack and make no garbage.

cards.q: Which of these remove allocations in a hot path? Select all that apply.
options: static readonly WaitForSeconds instead of new in a loop
for by index instead of foreach over IList<T>
A prebuilt array of "Clash 1"... strings
Calling GC.Collect() every frame
Moving the LINQ to a background thread
cards.explain: The first three remove the allocations themselves. GC.Collect every frame causes huge pauses, and you cannot move code that touches scene objects to a background thread.

cards.q: Match the problem to the fix
pairs: Reusable list and a plain loop
Array of ready strings, assign on change

cards.title: How to prove there is garbage
cards.body:
In a review, "I feel it is slow" is weak and "here is the number" is strong. Open Profiler → CPU, enable the GC Alloc column and look at a frame: how many bytes, and from where.

The rule: in a quiet frame with no events, GC Alloc should be 0. If it shows 2 KB per frame, that is already about 120 KB of garbage per second at 60 FPS.
cards.deep: Turn on Call Stacks in the profiler (Allocation Callstacks) to see exactly which line allocates. Deep Profile slows the game a lot and distorts timings, but it works for finding the source of allocations. For before/after comparisons, Profile Analyzer and Memory Profiler (snapshots before and after) are more convenient.

lessons.title: Materials and batching
lessons.sub: renderer.material, SRP Batcher, MaterialPropertyBlock, GPU Instancing

cards.title: A private paint can for every marker
cards.body:
A workshop has one shared palette: red paint and gray paint. Any marker walks up and takes what it needs. That is sharedMaterial.

Now imagine that the first time a marker asks to be painted, it is handed its own private can, poured from the shared one. There are a hundred cans, and nobody knows who will throw them away. That is renderer.material: the first access clones the material for that renderer (the name gets an "(Instance)" suffix).

Two troubles at once: the copies are not destroyed automatically, and every marker now has its own material, so the engine has a harder time merging them into one draw call.
cards.deep:
The Unity docs say it plainly: you are responsible for destroying materials created through .material (Destroy in OnDestroy). Destroying the GameObject does not destroy the copy. Only an unload of unused assets picks it up: Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets, or a Single-mode scene load (which runs the same unload), and only if nothing references the copy any more. In a long-lived scene where markers are created and destroyed, the copies pile up.

To be precise about batching: a copy breaks static and dynamic batching and GPU Instancing (they need the very same material). The SRP Batcher does merge different materials of one shader variant, but every copy needs its own property buffer in GPU memory. So in URP the main harm of .material is memory and the leak, not the batch count.

cards.task: Three methods paint markers. Find both different ways to do it badly.

bugs.title: Touching .material creates a copy
bugs.why: Every renderer gets a private material. The copies stay in memory until someone destroys them explicitly, and static batching, dynamic batching and instancing can no longer merge them.

bugs.title: sharedMaterial.color paints the shared material
bugs.why: You change the material itself: the color changes for everything that uses it. In the editor the change is even saved into the asset file.

cards.q: There are 100 markers in the scene and each one called renderer.material.color. How many materials live in memory now?
options: One: the material is shared
About a hundred copies plus the original
Two: red and gray
cards.explain: The first access to .material on each renderer clones the source material. The copies stay until someone destroys them or unused assets are unloaded.

wrong.0: The material stays shared only while you read .sharedMaterial.
wrong.2: You would get red and gray if we assigned two ready-made materials.

cards.title: What batching is
cards.body:
Every "draw this" command costs the CPU time. Batching merges commands so there are fewer of them.

Static works for objects that never move and have the Static flag. Dynamic: the CPU merges small meshes that share a material (small means roughly 300 vertices; it is off by default in URP). SRP Batcher, in URP and HDRP: objects with the same shader variant are drawn back to back without reconfiguring, and the material data already lives in GPU memory. It does not reduce the number of draw calls, but it makes each one much cheaper. GPU Instancing: one mesh and one material are drawn as a pack, and the values that differ go in an array.

The general idea: the more things are identical, the better they merge.

cards.title: Three right ways to paint
cards.body:
1. Two shared materials. Red and gray are set up in the inspector, and the code is just r.sharedMaterial = _red. No copies, no leak.

2. MaterialPropertyBlock (MPB). A note attached to the renderer: "use that material, but with a different color". No new material is created, so no leak.

3. GPU Instancing. One material and one mesh, while each instance has its own color through an instanced shader property.

An important catch: in a URP/HDRP project an MPB takes that renderer out of the SRP Batcher. Different materials on the same shader, though, batch fine in the SRP Batcher! So for red/gray on URP, two shared materials are usually the best choice.
cards.deep: In the Built-in RP, "MPB + GPU Instancing" is the classic pair: different property values do not break instancing. In URP, if a renderer is SRP Batcher compatible, the SRP Batcher is used (it has priority), and instancing picks up the renderers the SRP Batcher cannot take (for example, those with an MPB). Shader compatibility is shown in the shader inspector ("SRP Batcher: compatible"). For thousands of identical objects, newer Unity versions also have Graphics.RenderMeshInstanced and BatchRendererGroup, but that is a separate topic.

cards.q: A URP project, 500 markers, each either red or gray. What do you choose?
options: renderer.material.color on each one: "simpler"
A MaterialPropertyBlock on every renderer
Two shared materials on one shader and r.sharedMaterial = the right one
Destroy and recreate the material every frame
cards.explain: The SRP Batcher merges two shared materials on one shader with no trouble, and there are no copies.

wrong.0: That means 500 material copies and garbage in memory.
wrong.1: An MPB removes the renderer from the SRP Batcher: on URP that is worse than two materials.
wrong.3: The worst option: heavy work and memory fragmentation every frame.

cards.q: Assign ready-made materials, and leave the renderer alone if it already has the right one.
cards.explain: sharedMaterial reads and assigns the shared material without cloning. If we read .material for the comparison, the copy would already be created by the check.

cards.q: If you still need a MaterialPropertyBlock (Built-in RP or instancing), put the steps in order.
items: Once (in Awake), create the MaterialPropertyBlock in a field and get the property ID with Shader.PropertyToID
Read the renderer's current values: r.GetPropertyBlock(block)
Write the color: block.SetColor(id, color)
Apply it to the renderer: r.SetPropertyBlock(block)
cards.explain: The block and the ID are created once, so there is no garbage. After that the pattern is read, change, write.

cards.q: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The SRP Batcher can merge renderers with different materials on the same shader
MaterialPropertyBlock is compatible with the SRP Batcher
renderer.material clones the material, and you must destroy the copies yourself
MaterialPropertyBlock creates a new material
GPU Instancing draws instances that share one mesh and one material as a pack
cards.explain: An MPB does not create new materials, but renderers with a block drop out of the SRP Batcher.

cards.q: A URP project with the SRP Batcher on. Which line knocks the renderer out of the SRP Batcher?
cards.explain: A renderer with a MaterialPropertyBlock does not use the SRP Batcher (it goes through the regular path or instancing). The other lines do not affect batching.

cards.q: Match the approach to the situation
pairs: Very small meshes in the Built-in RP
URP/HDRP, many materials on one shader
Thousands of identical meshes with different colors
Different values on one material in the Built-in RP

cards.title: How to find a material leak
cards.body:
Open the Memory Profiler (or Profiler → Memory) and look at the material count. If it grows every time markers appear, some code uses .material. The copy names end with "(Instance)".

The Frame Debugger shows why batches did not merge: every draw call has a reason ("Objects have different materials" and so on).
cards.deep: A small detail: Material.color writes to the property marked with the [MainColor] attribute or named _Color. In URP Lit shaders that is _BaseColor, which is marked correctly, but with hand-written shaders you can get "nothing changes color". With SetColor by string you must give the right name. Cache the ID: Shader.PropertyToID("_BaseColor").

lessons.title: Lifecycle and flags
lessons.sub: OnEnable/OnDisable, dead objects, HasFlag and Camera.main

cards.title: A newsletter you can join but never leave
cards.body:
You subscribe to a newsletter every time you walk into a room, but you only unsubscribe when the house is demolished. You can leave and re-enter the room as often as you like, though: every entry is a new subscription, and the letters arrive in twos and threes.

In Unity a component has matching pairs: Awake → OnEnable → Start → … → OnDisable → OnDestroy. OnEnable and OnDisable fire every time the object is switched on and off (SetActive or enabled), while OnDestroy fires once, at the end. Subscribe in one place, unsubscribe in its pair.

cards.task: A piece of ClashMarkers about events, the coroutine and the marker list. Flag the lines with mistakes.

bugs.title: Subscribed in OnEnable, unsubscribed only in OnDestroy
bugs.why: After the object is switched off and on, the handler subscribes a second time and runs twice, and after enabled = false/true two copies of the coroutine are running. A disabled object also keeps receiving events.

bugs.title: GameObject list is never cleaned
bugs.why: A destroyed object stays in the list as a "fake null". Touching its transform throws MissingReferenceException and kills the coroutine.

bugs.title: new WaitForSeconds in a loop
bugs.why: A new object on every iteration, 20 times a second. One shared instance is enough.

bugs.title: HasFlag used for an "any of the flags" test
bugs.why: HasFlag needs all the bits you pass, and for None it always returns true. A filter on "overlaps" comes out wrong.

cards.title: What breaks on switch off and on
cards.body:
Call SetActive(false) and then SetActive(true). What happened: OnDisable ran, with no unsubscribe, then OnEnable added the delegate one more time. The event chain now holds two identical handlers. OnDestroy never ran at all.

The fix is symmetry: whatever you do in OnEnable, undo in OnDisable. Store the coroutine in a field and stop it.
cards.deep:
A subtlety with coroutines: SetActive(false) stops all coroutines on the object, but enabled = false on the component does not. The coroutine keeps running, and after enabled = true, OnEnable starts a second copy. So calling StopCoroutine explicitly in OnDisable is safer.

A static event also keeps its subscriber alive: until the subscriber unsubscribes, the reference stays (the GC cannot collect the C# object), and a destroyed component keeps getting calls. Its plain C# fields still read fine, but touching transform, gameObject or any other engine API throws MissingReferenceException.

cards.q: The object was switched off and on (SetActive(false), then SetActive(true)). How many times does OnSelected run for one ClashEvents.Selected event?
options: An exception is thrown
cards.explain: OnDestroy never ran, so the first subscription is still there. OnEnable added the same method a second time, and the delegate chain calls it twice.

wrong.0: Switching off does not remove the subscription, because there is no unsubscribe.
wrong.1: It would be once with a symmetric OnEnable and OnDisable.
wrong.3: Subscribing again throws nothing. It silently duplicates.

cards.q: Make the subscription symmetric and stop the coroutine.
cards.explain: OnDisable runs on every switch off and before destruction, so it fits unsubscribing. We stop the coroutine from the field explicitly, so it does not keep running after enabled = false.

cards.title: The Unity "fake null"
cards.body:
When you call Destroy(go), the C# wrapper object stays alive and the real object inside the engine disappears. It is an envelope with nothing in it. Any access to it, go.activeSelf or go.transform, throws MissingReferenceException.

Unity overloaded == so that go == null is true for that empty envelope. So the marker list needs cleaning: _markers.RemoveAll(m => m == null), or the marker reports its own destruction and removes itself from the list.
cards.deep:
Destroy is not instant: the object goes away at the end of the frame (DestroyImmediate is instant, but you should avoid it in gameplay code). The operators ?., ??, is null and ReferenceEquals bypass the overloaded ==, so they will not notice a destroyed object. Check with == null or if (obj).

You cannot modify a list during foreach: you get InvalidOperationException. Clean up outside the loop or with RemoveAll.

cards.q: Which check will NOT notice a destroyed GameObject m?
options: if (m == null)
if (!m)
if (m is null)
if (m != null && m.activeSelf)
cards.explain: The is null pattern checks the reference directly and does not call the Unity overloaded operator. The other options go through == or the implicit bool conversion and correctly see the "dead" object.

wrong.0: The overloaded == returns true for a destroyed object.
wrong.1: The ! operator also uses the Unity implicit conversion to bool.
wrong.3: Here != works through the overload, so m.activeSelf is never reached.

cards.title: Flags: [Flags] and HasFlag
cards.body:
An enum with [Flags] is a set of switches: Hard = 1, Soft = 2, Clearance = 4. The filter "Hard and Soft" equals 3 (011 in binary).

x.HasFlag(f) means (x & f) == f: all bits of f must be on. For a single flag that is the same as "is it set". But:

• HasFlag(None) is always true, because 0 is contained in everything.
• For the combination Hard | Clearance both bits are required.

If the question is "does at least one match", write (x & f) != 0.
cards.deep: Enum.HasFlag(Enum flag) takes its argument as an object and is called on a value type, so in Unity's Mono (and in IL2CPP, at least in older versions) every call boxes both the argument and the enum itself. That is allocation on every call. In .NET Core 2.1 and later the JIT recognizes HasFlag and turns it into a bitwise test with no boxing. The bitwise form is fast everywhere, so prefer it in hot Unity code.

cards.q: The filter is Hard | Soft (3). What does the call return?
cards.code:
var filter = ClashFilter.Hard | ClashFilter.Soft;
bool r = filter.HasFlag(ClashFilter.Hard | ClashFilter.Clearance);
options: true, because Hard is set
false, because Clearance is not in the filter
An exception
cards.explain: HasFlag needs every bit of the argument to be set. The Clearance bit is not set, so the result is false. For "any of", use (filter & mask) != 0.

wrong.0: That is the answer for "at least one" logic, but HasFlag uses "all" logic.
wrong.2: HasFlag does not throw.

cards.q: Rewrite the check: leave when the event shares no flag with the filter.
cards.code:
if ((_filter ___ type) ___ 0)
    return;
cards.explain: (_filter & type) keeps the shared bits. If the result is zero there are no common flags, and the event must be skipped.

cards.q: Which statements about the lifecycle are true? Select all that apply.
options: OnDisable runs both on SetActive(false) and before the object is destroyed
enabled = false on a component stops its coroutines
SetActive(false) on the object stops its coroutines
OnDestroy runs every time the object is switched off
cards.explain: enabled = false does not touch coroutines. OnDestroy runs once, when the object is destroyed.

cards.q: Match the symptom to the cause
pairs: The handler fires twice after switching off and on
Subscribed in OnEnable, unsubscribed in OnDestroy
MissingReferenceException while iterating the marker list
Destroyed objects stayed in the list
Zero is contained in every value
After enabled = false/true the profiler shows Pulse twice per step
The coroutine was not stopped and was started again

cards.title: Camera.main can be null
cards.body:
The code Camera.main.transform.position assumes the scene has an enabled camera with the MainCamera tag. If there is none (a UI-only scene, tests, a disabled camera), you get a NullReferenceException.

The fix: fetch the camera once, check it for null and return from the method instead of crashing.
cards.deep: One more thought for seniors: the markers in the listing are made with Instantiate and removed with Destroy (that code is not shown, but the markers are in the list). With hundreds of markers that is constant allocation and GC pressure. In such cases use an object pool: UnityEngine.Pool.ObjectPool<T> (available since Unity 2021.1) or your own. The marker is then switched off and returned to the pool instead of being destroyed, and the list of dead references never appears.

lessons.title: Cache and sorting
lessons.sub: The comparer contract and your own LRU thumbnail cache

cards.title: A judge who cannot call a tie
cards.body:
A sort asks the comparer: "which is bigger, a or b?" The answer is a number: less than zero (a goes first), zero (equal) or greater than zero (a goes later).

The answer has contract rules:

• Compare(x, x) equals 0.
• If Compare(a, b) < 0, then Compare(b, a) > 0.
• If a goes before b and b before c, then a goes before c.

The comparer in the listing, a.Severity > b.Severity ? -1 : 1, never says "zero". For two equal values it answers "a goes after b" in both directions. A judge with no ties.

cards.task: A sort and a thumbnail cache that should drop the pictures nobody has needed for the longest time (LRU). Find the mistakes.

bugs.title: The comparer never returns 0
bugs.why: The contract is broken: Compare(x, x) gives 1. The order rests on Sort implementation details, NaN in the data breaks it, and BinarySearch or SortedSet with this comparer will never find an equal element.

bugs.title: Get does not update the usage order
bugs.why: A picture you just read does not become "fresh". Even with correct eviction this would be a plain queue (FIFO), not an LRU: frequently used pictures get thrown out for nothing.

bugs.title: The newest element is evicted, not the oldest
bugs.why: AddLast puts the new element at the end, and the eviction takes Last too. The fresh picture goes on the very next Put, and the oldest ones stay forever.

bugs.title: Put with an id that is already cached
bugs.why: The id lands in _order a second time and the old entry is not removed, so the order drifts out of sync with _map. Later an eviction removes a live entry. The Count >= capacity check also fires on a simple update.

bugs.title: The evicted texture is never destroyed
bugs.why: Texture2D wraps native memory. The garbage collector will not free it: native memory leaks until someone destroys the texture by hand.

cards.title: What Sort really guarantees
cards.body:
When the contract is broken, List.Sort promises nothing: what happens depends on the implementation and on the data. That is why such a bug is "flaky".

• A comparer that answers −1 for equal values can drive the partition loop past the end of the array in .NET Framework and Unity's Mono, and Sort throws ArgumentException "Unable to sort because the IComparer.Compare() method returns inconsistent results".
• Ours answers +1 for equal values, and on ordinary numbers List.Sort happens to sort correctly. But a > NaN is always false, so with NaN in the data the order turns to garbage, with no exception at all.

The right descending comparer is b.Severity.CompareTo(a.Severity). It honestly returns 0 for equal values and handles NaN (NaN counts as smaller than any number).
cards.deep:
Why our comparer "works": the .NET introsort (both in Unity's Mono and in modern .NET) only compares the result with zero, and "+1 on ties" merely makes it swap equal elements now and then, which an unstable sort never promised to avoid anyway. That is an implementation detail, not a guarantee. In modern .NET the partition loops also check bounds, so the exception is rare there and only the silently wrong order remains. Code that needs an actual 0 (BinarySearch, SortedSet, SortedList) breaks at once with such a comparer: an equal element is never found.

List.Sort and Array.Sort use introsort, which is unstable: equal elements may swap places. If you need stability, use OrderByDescending (LINQ sorting is stable but allocates) or add a second key such as the original index. Another trap: a comparer like (int)(b.Severity - a.Severity) breaks the contract too, because the fractional part is cut off and different values become "equal" inconsistently.

cards.q: The tests for a comparer "greater gives minus one, otherwise plus one" are green: the list sorts correctly. What do you tell the author in review?
options: All good: the tests pass, so the comparer is correct
The contract is broken: the correct order rests on Sort implementation details, NaN in the data breaks it, and BinarySearch and SortedSet with this comparer will not find an equal element
List.Sort always throws on equal values; the tests just do not contain any
A sort with this comparer can loop forever
cards.explain: With a broken contract nothing is guaranteed. Today the .NET introsort survives +1 on ties: it merely swaps equal elements now and then. But once a NaN shows up, the implementation changes, or the comparer ends up in code that needs a 0, everything breaks.

wrong.0: The tests show it works on this data and this implementation. Correctness is guaranteed only for a comparer that follows the contract.
wrong.2: Not always. This particular comparer (+1 on ties) usually does not throw on ordinary numbers. The exception is typical of a comparer that returns −1 on ties.
wrong.3: There is no infinite loop here. The trouble is that the result is not guaranteed.

cards.q: Fix the comparer: sort by Severity descending without breaking the contract.
cards.code: scores.Sort((a, b) => ___.Severity.CompareTo(___.Severity));
cards.explain: CompareTo returns 0 for equal values and handles NaN. Swapping a and b gives descending order: the bigger value gets a negative result.

cards.q: You need a stable descending order by Severity: markers with equal values keep their original order. What do you pick?
options: scores.Sort with any correct comparer, because it is stable
OrderByDescending(s => s.Severity).ToList(), a stable sort (but it creates a new list)
Array.Sort, because it is stable
cards.explain: LINQ OrderBy/OrderByDescending are stable. If you cannot allocate, add a second key to the comparer: the original index.

wrong.0: List.Sort and Array.Sort are built on introsort and are unstable.
wrong.2: Array.Sort is unstable too.

cards.title: LRU: a shelf that cannot hold everything
cards.body:
You have a shelf for 3 things. A thing you just used goes near the edge. When you need space, you throw out the one deepest in the back, because it has gone unused the longest. That is LRU (Least Recently Used).

We need two things at once:
• A dictionary id → node, to find a picture in O(1).
• A linked list of nodes from fresh to old, to move a node to the front and drop the tail in O(1).

front → [7] → [3] → [9] ← tail

Every Get and every Put moves the node to the front. We always evict the tail (Last).

cards.q: Put the steps of the Put method in order.
items: Check whether this id is already in the dictionary
If it is, replace the texture, move the node to the front and return
If it is not and the cache is full, take the node at the tail (Last)
Remove it from the list and the dictionary, and destroy its texture
Create a node for the new id, put it at the front, store it in the dictionary
cards.explain: First handle updating an existing key (nothing needs evicting). Only for a new key do we check fullness. The new node is added after space has been freed.

cards.q: Write Get: the node that was read must become the freshest.
cards.explain: First detach the node from the list, then insert it at the front. After Remove the node belongs to no list, so AddFirst accepts it. All in O(1).

cards.q: Write the eviction: remove the oldest picture and free its memory.
cards.explain: The least recently used node sits at the tail of the list, which is Last. A Texture2D must be destroyed explicitly (Destroy), or native memory leaks.

cards.title: The finished cache
cards.body: Here is the result: all the steps together. Read it and find where each bug from the listing is closed.
cards.deep: More to keep in mind. Ownership: the cache destroys textures, so a picture the UI is showing at that moment will vanish; agree on who owns it. Threads: Texture2D and the Unity API work only on the main thread, so the cache can stay lock-free, but access from other threads needs synchronization or a queue. Capacity: you can count bytes (width × height × format) instead of pictures. With a byte limit, evict in a loop until the new item fits.

cards.q: Capacity is 3. On the old (broken) cache you call Put(1), Put(2), Put(3), Put(4). What is in it now?
cards.explain: After three Puts the order is 1, 2, 3 and Last is 3. The 3 is evicted (the newest element) and 4 is added. What remains is 1, 2, 4: the oldest entry, 1, stays forever.

wrong.0: That is the result of a correct FIFO/LRU: the oldest element, 1, would go.
wrong.2: The fourth Put still adds element 4.

cards.q: Match the cache bug to its symptom
pairs: Get does not move the node
The cache behaves like FIFO, not LRU
The fresh picture is thrown out at once
Put of an existing id with no check
A duplicate in _order and drift from the dictionary

lessons.title: Finale: ClashMarkers
lessons.sub: A full review of the class: memory, speed, lifecycle

cards.task: The full ClashMarkers and ThumbnailCache listing. Find as many problems as you can: allocations, materials, lifecycle, flags, comparer, cache.

bugs.title: LINQ chain in Update
bugs.why: Every frame, Where, OrderBy and ToList create iterators, a sort buffer and a new list: steady garbage and regular GC pauses.

bugs.title: Camera.main and Vector3.Distance inside the sort key
bugs.why: The camera is fetched for every marker every frame (a tag lookup in old Unity versions), and Distance does a square root. Read the position once and compare sqrMagnitude. If there is no camera, you get a NullReferenceException.

bugs.title: GetComponent for every visible marker every frame
bugs.why: An expensive lookup you could do once when the marker is created, keeping the reference.

bugs.title: renderer.material makes a copy of the material
bugs.why: Every marker gets a private material: the copies are not destroyed along with the object (a leak), and static/dynamic batching and instancing can no longer merge them. Use two shared materials (red and gray) or, outside the SRP Batcher, a MaterialPropertyBlock.

bugs.title: String and TextMesh work every frame, plus GetComponentInChildren
bugs.why: Concatenation makes garbage for every marker, and assigning text every frame may rebuild the TextMesh mesh even though the text did not change. Cache the reference, use prebuilt strings and assign only on change.

bugs.title: Subscription and coroutine in OnEnable, unsubscribe only in OnDestroy
bugs.why: After the object is switched off and on, the handler is added a second time and fires twice, and after enabled = false/true two coroutines run. The static event also keeps the disabled object alive. You need OnEnable/OnDisable symmetry and a stopped coroutine.

bugs.title: new WaitForSeconds in the coroutine loop
bugs.why: A new allocation 20 times a second. One static readonly instance is enough.

bugs.title: GameObject list is never cleaned
bugs.why: Destroyed objects stay in the list as a "fake null", and touching them (activeSelf, transform) throws MissingReferenceException. Clean the list (RemoveAll(m => m == null)) or manage marker lifetime through a pool.

bugs.title: HasFlag instead of an overlap test
bugs.why: HasFlag needs all bits and is always true for None, and in Unity's Mono it also boxes. (_filter & type) != 0 is safer.

bugs.title: The comparer never returns 0
bugs.why: The contract is broken (Compare(x, x) = 1): the order rests on Sort implementation details, NaN turns it into garbage, and BinarySearch/SortedSet with this comparer will not find an equal element. Use b.Severity.CompareTo(a.Severity).

bugs.title: foreach over IList<T> boxes the enumerator
bugs.why: Every call allocates. Better to accept List<T> or IReadOnlyList<T> and loop with for by index.

bugs.title: Get does not update the order
bugs.why: A thumbnail you just read does not become "fresh": the cache works as FIFO, not LRU.

bugs.title: The newest element is evicted, not the oldest
bugs.why: AddLast puts the new id at the end and the eviction takes Last too: the fresh picture goes on the next Put, and the old ones stay forever.

bugs.title: Put with an id that is already cached
bugs.why: The id lands in _order twice, the old entry stays, and the order drifts out of sync with the dictionary. The eviction also fires on a simple update.

bugs.title: The evicted Texture2D is never destroyed
bugs.why: It wraps native memory: the GC will not free it, so memory leaks until Destroy is called.

bugs.title: Capacity 0 is not validated
bugs.why: With capacity = 0, the first Put finds _order.Last equal to null and throws NullReferenceException. The constructor should reject a non-positive capacity.

cards.q: Which statements about the original ClashMarkers are true? Select all that apply.
options: renderer.material in Update gives every marker its own copy of the material
If an event arrives with ClashFilter.None, HasFlag returns true and the filter lets it through
After enabled = false the Pulse coroutine stops by itself
The garbage collector will free a Texture2D evicted from the cache
Putting the same id again leaves a duplicate in _order
cards.explain: SetActive(false) stops coroutines, enabled = false does not. Only Destroy or an unload of unused assets frees the native memory of a Texture2D; the GC does not touch it.

cards.q: In the profiler, the material count grows every time the markers are recreated. How do you check that these are copies from .material?
options: Look at the material names in the Memory Profiler: copies have an "(Instance)" suffix
Call GC.Collect() and see whether they disappear
Rename the material in the project
cards.explain: Copies made through .material are named "Name (Instance)". GC.Collect will not remove them: they are Unity objects, destroyed with Destroy or by unloading unused assets.

wrong.1: Collecting the managed heap does not free Unity objects.
wrong.2: The name of the source material does not affect the copies.

cards.q: Which line breaks the comparer contract (Compare(x, x) is not zero)?
cards.explain: For equal values the first line answers 1 in both directions, and it can never return zero. The second and third use CompareTo, which returns 0 for equal values.

cards.q: Put the component lifecycle calls in order, from creation to destruction (the object is active the whole time, then it is destroyed).
items: Awake
OnEnable
Start
Update
OnDisable
OnDestroy
cards.explain: Awake and OnEnable run when an active object is created, and Start runs before the first Update. When an active object is destroyed, OnDisable runs first, then OnDestroy.

cards.q: To compare "who is closer" you do not need the root. Fill in the blank.
cards.code: float d = (a.position - b.position).___;
cards.explain: The squared distance rises and falls exactly like the distance, but needs no square root.

cards.q: Which tool for which job?
pairs: Find which line makes garbage in a frame
See why batches did not merge
Estimate the number of draw calls

cards.q: The cache evicts a Texture2D without calling Destroy: "the garbage collector will free it anyway". Why is that a mistake?
options: The GC frees only the managed wrapper object; the native texture memory stays until it is destroyed or unused assets are unloaded
You must never evict a Texture2D from a dictionary
Destroy is needed only in the editor
cards.explain: Texture2D is a thin wrapper over native data. The managed heap and native memory follow different rules.

wrong.1: You can evict it. The question is releasing the resources.
wrong.2: In a build, native memory leaks in exactly the same way.
